item.title: AI Agents Collaborate, Rare-Earth-Free Magnets Found: Materials Discovery Accelerates
item.description: This comprehensive review covers 26 articles published in January 2026, surveying the latest developments in materials discovery. Multiple autonomous AI systems learned to work together spontaneously, sharing distilled knowledge rather than raw data to optimize materials exploration faster than any single system could achieve alone. Meanwhile, researchers used combinatorial methods to create high-entropy boride magnets that eliminate the need for critical rare-earth elements, and AI-driven frameworks identified shape-memory alloys with record efficiency. The field’s data infrastructure continues to scale dramatically.
item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 26 articles published in January 2026, surveying the latest developments in materials discovery. Multiple autonomous AI systems learned to work together spontaneously, sharing distilled knowledge rather than raw data to optimize materials exploration faster than any single system could achieve alone. Meanwhile, researchers used combinatorial methods to create high-entropy boride magnets that eliminate the need for critical rare-earth elements, and AI-driven frameworks identified shape-memory alloys with record efficiency. The field’s data infrastructure continues to scale dramatically.

The Big Story: AI Agents Learn to Collaborate

Researchers from the National Institute for Materials Science and University of Tsukuba have demonstrated an autonomous AI network where multiple AI systems spontaneously collaborate to discover new materials more efficiently . In simulations, three autonomous AI systems shared knowledge and improved optimization speed, enhancing exploration efficiency in ways that mimic human research communication patterns .

The key innovation is that these systems share distilled knowledge rather than raw data. This approach, described as “hierarchical autonomous materials search” in the research published December 2025 in npj Computational Materials, allows collective acceleration of materials exploration beyond what individual systems can achieve. The algorithm enables multiple AI agents to learn from each other’s discoveries without transferring massive datasets, instead communicating higher-level insights about promising regions of the search space.

Building on this theme of human-machine collaboration, researchers from Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering proposed an “AI advisor” model that helps scientists steer autonomous labs like Polybot published in Nature Chemical Engineering . When applied to discovering mixed ion-electron conducting polymers, this collaborative approach achieved a 150% performance improvement over previous cutting-edge techniques. The AI advisor provides an adaptive decision interface that enhances both efficiency and deep understanding in material science, demonstrating that human expertise combined with autonomous systems can outperform either approach alone.

These developments point to a broader shift: AI is moving from a prediction tool to an active research collaborator. The autonomous AI network technology demonstrates that machines can coordinate their own exploration strategies, while the AI advisor model shows how human scientists can effectively guide and interpret autonomous experimental systems.

Materials Breakthroughs

Sustainable Magnets Without Rare Earths

Researchers at Georgetown University have discovered a new class of strong magnets based on high-entropy borides that use only earth-abundant transition metals and boron, avoiding rare-earth and precious metals entirely . The materials, published in Advanced Materials in 2025 under the title “C16 Phase High Entropy Borides With High Magnetic Anisotropy,” exhibit significant magnetic anisotropy—a critical property for permanent magnets.

High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements in near-equal proportions, creating unique properties that emerge from the chemical complexity rather than from a single dominant element. The research team led by Professors Kai Liu and Gen Yin used a combinatorial sputtering method that can create 50 samples simultaneously on a single substrate, enabling rapid exploration of the vast compositional space. This high-throughput approach was essential for identifying promising compositions among the many possible combinations.

The discovery matters because rare-earth elements like neodymium and dysprosium are critical for motors, robotics, data storage, and MRI machines, but their supply is geopolitically concentrated and extraction is environmentally damaging. High-entropy borides offer a potential path to sustainable magnets that rely only on abundant materials. The C16 phase crystal structure (tetragonal) provides the structural foundation for the magnetic properties observed.

Record-Efficient Shape-Memory Alloy

Researchers at Texas A&M University, funded by the National Science Foundation, used an AI materials selection framework to discover a new shape-memory alloy with the highest operational efficiency ever recorded for nickel-titanium-base materials according to Cutting Tool Engineering . The alloy exhibits the narrowest hysteresis ever recorded, meaning minimal energy loss during thermal-to-mechanical conversion.

Shape-memory alloys, first developed in the mid-1960s, return to a predetermined shape when heated, making them useful for actuators, medical devices, and other applications. The traditional Ni-Ti-Cu system typically uses 50% titanium, but the AI framework identified a composition with 47% titanium and 21% copper that delivers superior performance. The team used a vacuum arc melter for experimental validation, confirming the AI’s predictions.

This data-driven approach offers proof of concept for accelerating future materials development. Professor Ibrahim Karaman, head of the materials science and engineering department, and doctoral student William Trehern demonstrated that machine learning can navigate compositional spaces more efficiently than traditional trial-and-error methods. The narrow hysteresis means the alloy wastes less energy during each thermal cycle, making it more practical for applications that require repeated actuation.

Other Notable Discoveries

Researchers at the Institute of Science Tokyo developed APF-80, a new metal-organic framework (MOF) that enhances the crystalline sponge method for molecular structure analysis according to research published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society . The crystalline sponge method allows X-ray diffraction analysis of molecules without growing single crystals—a notoriously difficult step for many compounds. APF-80’s improved stability, achieved through synergistic coordination and hydrogen bonding, allows it to visualize complex alkaloids and other reactive compounds without degradation. This advancement accelerates pharmaceutical research and has potential applications in fragrances, catalysts, and energy materials.

In optics, Harvard University researchers discovered that silica (silicon dioxide), a low-refractive-index material, can be effectively used to create optical metasurfaces challenging the field’s preference for high-index materials . Led by Professor Federico Capasso, the team found that silica metasurfaces operating in a single-mode regime offer robustness to fabrication errors and compatibility with standard chip-making processes like photolithography and electron beam lithography. The work, published in Nano Letters in 2025, demonstrates high-performance flat optics including lenses and gratings, potentially enabling more scalable and cost-effective optical devices.

Researchers at TU Wien and Rice University discovered a new topological state of matter in the quantum-critical material CeRu\(_4\)Sn\(_6\) published in Nature Physics . This “emergent topological semimetal” exhibits a spontaneous Hall effect without an external magnetic field, observed at temperatures less than one degree above absolute zero. The discovery challenges the previous understanding that topological properties require a classical particle picture of electrons, indicating that topological states are more general than previously thought and suggesting a new strategy for finding topological materials in quantum-critical systems. The work was led by Prof. Silke Bühler-Paschen at TU Wien and Prof. Qimiao Si at Rice University, with first authors Diana Kirschbaum and Lei Chen.

Computational Methods & Tools

Generative Design

Researchers from New York University, the University of Florida, the University of Minnesota, and Brigham Young University developed PropMolFlow (Property-guided Molecular Flow), an AI model that designs molecules with specified properties roughly 10 times faster than previous methods according to NYU . The approach generates chemically valid, targeted molecular structures in approximately 100 computational steps, compared to 1,000 for previous methods. The model generated molecules with correct bonding patterns and geometries in more than 90% of cases.

PropMolFlow works “backward” from desired properties to molecular structure, an inverse design approach that dramatically reduces the computational steps needed to find candidate molecules. The research, funded by the National Science Foundation and the Simons Center for Computational Physical Chemistry at NYU, could accelerate the discovery of new pharmaceuticals and advanced materials. Assistant Professor Stefano Martiniani of NYU and Assistant Professor Mingjie Liu of the University of Minnesota led the work.

A comprehensive review in Nature Materials surveys the evolution of AI-driven computational techniques for materials design, highlighting the paradigm shift from traditional screening methods to inverse design powered by deep generative models authored by Han et al., 2025 . The review covers key advances including high-throughput machine learning, evolutionary algorithms, reinforcement learning, and generative models such as generative adversarial nets (GANs), variational autoencoders (VAE), and denoising diffusion probabilistic models. It also discusses foundation models for atomistic materials, crystal graph convolutional neural networks (CGCNN), and neural network potentials like CHGNet, while addressing current challenges in data scarcity and computational cost.

Active Learning & Integration

Researchers from Chalmers University of Technology developed an active learning approach combining machine learning interatomic potentials and first-principles calculations to discover high entropy oxides for chemical looping processes reports Quantum Zeitgeist . The team identified promising oxygen carrier materials based on perovskites like CaMnO\(_3\), using techniques including Gaussian processes, Wasserstein auto-encoder neural networks, and Monte Carlo dropout for uncertainty quantification. This approach accelerates materials discovery for sustainable technologies such as carbon capture and efficient energy production. The research team included Joakim Brorsson, Henrik Klein Moberg, Joel Hildingsson, Jonatan Gastaldi, Tobias Mattisson, and Anders Hellman.

Researchers from the China University of Petroleum (East China) published a comprehensive review on integrating artificial intelligence with density functional theory to accelerate materials discovery and design according to EurekAlert! . The AI-DFT framework enables a closed-loop, data-driven approach that shifts from traditional trial-and-error methods, improving efficiency and enabling active design. The review highlights applications in semiconductors, perovskites, and 2D materials, demonstrating faster property prediction and candidate screening. Techniques covered include random forests, convolutional neural networks, generative adversarial networks, and active learning.

Microsoft’s MatterGen and MatterSim initiatives exemplify the shift from academic research to commercial application in AI-driven materials science according to Analytics Insight . These platforms use machine learning models to predict material properties and simulate experiments, reducing years of trial-and-error to weeks or months. This transformation enables faster innovation in critical sectors like energy, manufacturing, semiconductors, and pharmaceuticals, with major initiatives from both Microsoft and Google driving the field forward.

Data Infrastructure

The Materials Project, a large open-access materials database from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, has grown to over 650,000 registered users and is now critical infrastructure powering the AI revolution in materials science according to Newswise . The platform has been cited 32,000 times across the literature and delivered 465 terabytes of data to users in the last two years alone. Its database contains 200,000 materials and 577,000 molecules, with curated, machine-learning-ready datasets that enable researchers and companies to rapidly discover new materials for batteries, catalysts, and other technologies without extensive preprocessing.

The Materials Project’s impact is demonstrated by widespread industry adoption and major contributions. In 2023, Google DeepMind contributed nearly 400,000 new compounds from its GNoME (graph networks for materials exploration) project. The platform’s cloud infrastructure maintains 99.98% uptime and serves approximately 5,000 daily users. Launched in 2011 with 120,000 users by early 2020, the platform has grown 2.5 times since May 2022, reflecting the surging demand for AI-ready materials data. Director Kristin Persson, Associate Director Anubhav Jain, and Technical Lead Patrick Huck lead the project, which has received support from the Toyota Research Institute, Microsoft Azure Quantum, and the Department of Energy’s Office of Science.

Complementing the Materials Project, researchers at the National Institute for Materials Science developed Research Data Express (RDE), a flexible data management system that automatically processes and structures materials science data according to Phys.org . Since its launch in January 2023, RDE has gained over 5,000 users with 16,000 datasets and 3 million data files. The system implements 1,900 Dataset Templates for various experimental methods, reducing the burden on researchers and enhancing data findability and reusability in alignment with FAIR principles. Researcher Jun Fujima led the development, with a paper published in Science and Technology of Advanced Materials: Methods in 2025.

Industry & Funding

Cambium has secured $100 million in Series B funding led by 8VC to accelerate the discovery and scaling of advanced materials according to PR Newswire . The round included participation from MVP Ventures, Lockheed Martin Ventures, GSBackers, Veteran Ventures Capital, J17 Ventures, and others. Cambium uses AI, chemical informatics, and high-performance computing to design new monomers and polymers hundreds of times faster than traditional methods, with applications in aerospace, defense, and other high-performance sectors. The funding will boost product pipeline and manufacturing in the U.S. and Europe, with CEO Simon Waddington leading the company’s expansion.

Revvity unveiled Signals Xynthetica, an AI-augmented platform for molecular and materials discovery that integrates computational modeling with experimental data to enable predictive, data-driven design reports Labmate-Online . The platform features in-silico generation, predictive modeling, experimental validation, models-as-a-service, de novo molecular design, property prediction, and multi-objective optimization. Early access programs are planned for the first half of 2026.

StartUs Insights published a comprehensive analysis of top material trends for 2026 and beyond, identifying AI material generators, 3D printing materials, and circular economy principles as key drivers reshaping product development according to their innovation guide . The global materials market is projected to reach $121.76 billion by 2033 with a 5.92% compound annual growth rate. The generative AI in material science market is expected to grow from $1.68 billion in 2025 to $5.35 billion in 2029, representing a 33.6% CAGR. The circular economy market is projected to grow from $517.79 billion to $798.3 billion by 2029 at an 11.4% CAGR. The report analyzed 10,300+ global startups and scaleups.

In a separate report, StartUs Insights highlighted 10 promising materials informatics startups to watch in 2026, showcasing their use of AI and data-driven approaches to accelerate material discovery and development according to their company analysis . The materials informatics sector is projected to reach $410.4 million by 2030 with an estimated 19.2% CAGR. Notable startups include Polaron (microstructural imaging and 3D reconstruction), EcoForge (AI-driven sustainable materials), fibclick (computational chemistry for pultrusion), AI Materia (high-throughput screening), and Aionics (AI for battery materials). The report identified 449 materials informatics startups overall.

StartUs Insights also surveyed 10 emerging AI solutions for material science, showcasing how startups are leveraging AI, machine learning, and quantum computing to accelerate innovation and sustainability according to their analysis . Notable companies include Elytra Biomaterials (digital twins for biopolymer production), Futur-AI (GPU-accelerated workflows), Atomic Tessellator (AI for porous materials design), Synboli (AI-driven MOF design), and Planck Technologies (quantum computing for materials simulation). The report identified 1,850 AI solutions for material science startups from a broader analysis of 9 million startups.

The World Economic Forum published an analysis emphasizing that AI’s true potential in materials discovery depends on pairing innovation with circular systems that keep existing materials in use according to their forum article . Achieving net zero by 2050 will require 6.5 billion tonnes of materials. The article notes that materials science papers mentioning AI or machine learning grew from 264 in 2014 to nearly 10,000 in 2024—a nearly 38-fold increase. Embodied carbon represents 20% of a typical data centre’s total lifecycle emissions, rising to nearly 100% when powered entirely by renewable electricity. The forum argues that AI-driven innovation must be aligned with new business models, infrastructure, and a focus on reducing the overall footprint of material extraction.

Eindhoven University of Technology secured 1.5 million euros for a European AI project in materials science according to the university news . A market insights report on generative AI in the chemical industry highlights the technology’s role in accelerating the discovery of new chemical entities and materials according to openPR.com .

Recognition

Physicists Pablo Jarillo-Herrero of MIT and Allan MacDonald of the University of Texas at Austin won the BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Award for their discovery of the “magic angle” in graphene layers reports EL PAÍS English . The €400,000 prize recognizes work that led to the field of twistronics, enabling control over electronic properties by rotating graphene layers to approximately 1.1 degrees relative to each other. MacDonald theoretically predicted the effect in 2011, and Jarillo-Herrero experimentally confirmed it in a landmark 2018 Nature paper. This breakthrough allows graphene to be turned into superconducting or insulating materials, with potential applications in quantum computing, infrared light detectors, and neurological computing.

Analysis of critical materials research reveals that China leads with 24.1% of global rare earth element publications and over 25,000 patents filed between 1950 and 2018 according to Discovery Alert . The United States holds 11.7% of publications, with a 2.5:1 Chinese-to-US patent filing ratio. An analysis of 76,768 peer-reviewed papers published between 1975 and 2024 shows annual publication volume growing from fewer than 100 papers in early years to 5,000 papers per year currently. Research focus shifted from geological exploration (1975-1990) to materials science applications (1990-2008) to accelerated and diversified research post-2008 following China’s export restrictions and the emergence of clean energy technologies.

Looking Ahead

The developments from January 2026 reveal a clear pattern: AI is moving from prediction to collaboration in materials science. The autonomous AI network breakthrough shows that multiple systems can coordinate their exploration strategies, sharing distilled insights rather than raw data. Combined with comprehensive data infrastructure—the Materials Project’s 650,000 users, 465 TB of data delivery, and 200,000 computed materials—and significant funding inflows like Cambium’s $100 million Series B, the field is accelerating rapidly.

The rare-earth-free magnet discovery demonstrates how computational approaches can solve critical supply chain challenges, while the shape-memory alloy breakthrough shows AI’s ability to navigate compositional spaces more efficiently than traditional methods. As the World Economic Forum analysis emphasizes, the greatest impact will come when AI-driven discovery is paired with circular systems that keep materials in use—aligning technological acceleration with sustainability imperatives.

The trajectory is clear: materials discovery is becoming a data-driven, AI-augmented discipline where autonomous systems collaborate with human scientists, databases provide machine-ready infrastructure, and funding flows toward platforms that can scale from prediction to production. The question is no longer whether AI can accelerate materials discovery, but how quickly the field can transition from identifying promising candidates to scaling them for commercial applications.

item.title: Quantum Computing's Security Awakening: 2026 Ushers in the Era of Quantum Defense
item.description: This comprehensive review covers 165 articles published in January 2026, surveying a field undergoing a profound shift. Federal agencies have declared 2026 the “Year of Quantum Security,” the Ethereum Foundation has formed a dedicated post-quantum security team with $2 million in research prizes, and a Jefferies strategist has removed Bitcoin from his model portfolio over quantum threats. Meanwhile, error correction researchers achieve 10,000x reductions in error rates, neutral-atom systems scale toward 100,000-qubit architectures, and the University of Waterloo launches the world’s first open-source full-stack quantum computer. Quantum computing is graduating from laboratory curiosity to infrastructure that must be secured, scaled, and democratized.
item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 165 articles published in January 2026, surveying a field undergoing a profound shift. Federal agencies have declared 2026 the “Year of Quantum Security,” the Ethereum Foundation has formed a dedicated post-quantum security team with $2 million in research prizes, and a Jefferies strategist has removed Bitcoin from his model portfolio over quantum threats. Meanwhile, error correction researchers achieve 10,000x reductions in error rates, neutral-atom systems scale toward 100,000-qubit architectures, and the University of Waterloo launches the world’s first open-source full-stack quantum computer. Quantum computing is graduating from laboratory curiosity to infrastructure that must be secured, scaled, and democratized.

The Security Awakening

2026 has been designated the “Year of Quantum Security” by the FBI and NIST, marking a coordinated shift from theoretical concerns to operational mandates across federal agencies source . A launch event in Washington, D.C. on January 12 brought together federal agencies including the White House, DHS, and CISA to address what officials call the “harvest now, decrypt later” threat—where adversaries steal encrypted data today intending to decrypt it once quantum computers mature source .

The urgency is translating into action. The Ethereum Foundation formed a dedicated Post-Quantum security team and announced the $1 million Poseidon Prize to strengthen the network’s quantum-resistant hash function. Combined with last year’s $1 million Proximity Prize for broader post-quantum research, the foundation has committed $2 million to blockchain defense source . Vitalik Buterin, Ethereum’s co-founder, estimates a 20% probability that quantum computers break current cryptography before 2030.

The financial sector is responding. Christopher Wood, Global Head of Equity Strategy at Jefferies, removed the 10% Bitcoin allocation from his recommended portfolio, replacing it with gold, citing concerns that quantum computing could crack cryptocurrency encryption source . Coinbase formed an Independent Advisory Board on Quantum Computing and Blockchain , bringing in experts including Dan Boneh of Stanford and Scott Aaronson to assess risks source . The board’s first position paper is expected early next year source .

Yet awareness has not translated into preparedness. 56% of mid-sized organizations admit they are not prepared for quantum threats source . Research from Bain & Company finds that 90% of companies lack systems to defend against quantum security threats, while 71% expect attacks within five years source . Only 10% have a roadmap to address quantum risks source .

Bitcoin developers maintain that threats are years away, noting slow progress in quantum computing and ongoing work on post-quantum cryptography source . But the divergence between enterprise anxiety and enterprise preparation is stark. As one analyst put it, companies focused narrowly on AI risk missing the quantum shift source .

The Security Paradox

Even as organizations mobilize against quantum threats to encryption, researchers have exposed a irony: quantum computers themselves have serious security flaws. Researchers at Penn State identified serious security weaknesses in current quantum computing systems, including vulnerabilities in program verification, circuit design, and hardware crosstalk source .

The research, funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and Intel, found that current security methods for classical computers are inadequate for quantum systems source . Swaroop Ghosh, professor of computer science and electrical engineering at Penn State, warns that as quantum computers become more integrated into industry, these flaws could expose sensitive corporate and personal information to theft and tampering source .

The vulnerabilities span multiple layers. Circuit topology issues could enable information encoding tampering, while hardware crosstalk between adjacent qubits could facilitate information leakage source . The researchers argue that protecting quantum computers requires securing both software and physical hardware from the ground up—a multi-layered defense strategy that current systems largely lack source .

This creates a paradox: quantum computing is viewed as an offensive threat to existing encryption, yet quantum systems themselves are vulnerable to attack. As industry adoption grows, addressing these foundational security challenges will be essential before quantum computers can be safely deployed for sensitive commercial and research applications source .

Error Correction Breakthroughs

The technical community is actively addressing quantum computing’s central challenge: error correction. Several advances this month demonstrate real progress toward fault-tolerant systems.

Cat Qubit Advances

Alice & Bob announced “Elevator Codes” , a new approach to error correction for cat qubit quantum computers source . The technique uses code concatenation to achieve a 10,000 times lower logical error rate compared to current error correction methods, requiring only 3 times more qubits source .

Diego Ruiz, theoretical physicist at Alice & Bob, notes that this reduction could enable complex molecular simulations sooner than expected source . The company, which has raised €130 million and hired 150 employees, claims its approach reduces hardware requirements for a large-scale quantum computer by 200 times source .

AI-Assisted Decoding

EdenCode emerged from stealth with $1.3 million in pre-seed funding to develop a real-time AI decoder for quantum error correction source . The San Jose-based startup, founded by Dr. Wanda Hou (CEO) and Prof. Yi-Zhuang You of UC San Diego, claims its hardware-agnostic neural network achieves a 99.9% error-detection rate and operates up to 10 times faster than conventional methods source .

The technology aims to reduce error rates by a factor of 10 and processes faults in less than a millisecond source . This addresses a critical bottleneck: as quantum systems scale, decoding delays can increase, but EdenCode’s approach is designed to scale without increasing processing time source .

Research & Tools

The snaQCs2025 project, a German consortium including neQxt GmbH, Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Solid State Physics IAF, and Point 8 GmbH, launched with €2.5 million in government funding to advance quantum error correction with logical qubits source . The three-year project aims to create a complete development pipeline from simulation to hardware integration source .

Nature published a demonstration of low-overhead quantum error correction codes, representing peer-reviewed validation of progress in the field source .

Microsoft released an updated, open-source Quantum Development Kit focused on creating fault-tolerant quantum applications source . The release includes specialized toolkits for chemistry and error correction, with the full error correction suite expected by late 2026 source . The kit integrates Visual Studio Code and GitHub Copilot to simplify quantum programming source .

Scaling Up: Hardware Advances

Neutral-Atom Scaling

Neutral-atom quantum computing emerged as a leading platform for scaling this month. Researchers at Columbia University demonstrated a new method combining optical tweezers with metasurfaces, successfully trapping 1,000 strontium atoms and creating a metasurface capable of generating 360,000 optical tweezers source . This lays groundwork for quantum computers with over 100,000 qubits source .

The approach overcomes bulk and cost limitations of previous technologies like spatial light modulators source . For comparison, a Caltech team achieved 6,100 trapped atoms using previous methods source . The Columbia team’s metasurface uses 200 nm pixels—smaller than the wavelength of light—and tolerates optical intensities up to 2,000 W/mm² source . The research was published in Nature source .

Moscow State University and Rosatom successfully tested a 72-qubit neutral-atom quantum computer prototype , utilizing rubidium atoms in optical tweezers with a novel three-zone architecture source . The system achieved 94% two-qubit gate accuracy, fulfilling a 2024 government mandate to scale neutral-atom platforms beyond 50 qubits source . Russia is targeting fault-tolerant quantum systems by 2030 source .

Silicon Progress

Researchers in Australia demonstrated an 11-qubit quantum processor using phosphorus atoms in isotopically-pure silicon-28, achieving gate fidelities above 99% source . The system operates at 16 mK and successfully created entangled states of up to eight atoms without performance degradation as qubits were added source .

This silicon-based approach shows promise for easier scaling than superconducting or ion-trap qubits, as it leverages existing semiconductor manufacturing expertise source . The work was published in Nature in 2025 source .

Commercial Deployments

Rigetti Computing received an $8.4 million order to deliver a 108-qubit quantum computer to India’s Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) source . The system, featuring Rigetti’s chiplet-based architecture, is scheduled for on-premises deployment in Bengaluru in the second half of 2026 source . This builds on a memorandum of understanding signed in September 2025 focused on hybrid quantum-classical computing systems source .

Rigetti’s superconducting systems operate with gate speeds of 50-70ns, which the company notes is approximately 1,000 times faster than ion traps and neutral atoms source . The company has previously sold systems with up to 180 qubits source .

The deployment is part of India’s broader quantum initiatives. The country’s National Quantum Mission has a budget of approximately $730 million source . Domestic developments include QpiAI’s 25-qubit Indus system, with a 64-qubit Kaveri processor planned source .

Capital Flows to Quantum

Equal1, an Irish quantum semiconductor company, raised $60 million (€51 million) in a funding round led by the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund source . The company’s Bell-1 QPU uses silicon spin qubits built on standard silicon, enabling integration with existing data centers source . The funds will support deployment in European HPC centers and acceleration of the roadmap toward millions of on-chip qubits source . A key deployment is planned for the European Space Agency’s High Performance Compute Centre source . Equal1’s CMOS-manufactured hybrid quantum-classical silicon-on-chip (QSoC) architecture aims to reduce cost and infrastructure barriers source .

Photonic, a Canadian quantum computing company, secured $130 million ($180M CAD) in funding led by Planet First Partners, bringing total capital raised to $271 million ($375M CAD) source . The company is developing fault-tolerant systems combining silicon-based qubits with photonic connectivity using its “Entanglement First Architecture” source . The funding will advance product milestones, expand teams, and deepen customer engagements source .

Microsoft launched the 2026 Quantum Research Pioneers Program (QuPP) , inviting academic researchers to submit proposals for funding up to $200,000 to advance measurement-based approaches for topological quantum computing source . The program focuses on challenges including simulation methods, error correction, and control techniques, with funding decisions announced March 15 and the program beginning August 1, 2026 source .

Democratizing Quantum Access

The University of Waterloo launched Open Quantum Design (OQD) , the world’s first open-source, full-stack quantum computer using ion-trapping technology source . OQD provides open access to quantum hardware and software, partnering with Haiqu, Unitary Foundation, and Xanadu to accelerate quantum computing development source . The initiative has 30 software contributors and builds on 8 years of hardware development at the Institute for Quantum Computing (IQC) source .

Co-founders Crystal Senko, Rajibul Islam, and Roger Melko aim to promote collaboration by providing real hardware access for algorithm testing source . This open-source model could accelerate quantum computing development by enabling broader collaboration source .

Sri Lanka inaugurated its first quantum computer , a nuclear magnetic resonance-powered system from Spinqiu housed at the University of Colombo source . The facility will enable hands-on learning and advanced research in quantum mechanics, positioning the country on the global quantum innovation map source .

Colorado School of Mines launched the first undergraduate Bachelor of Science in Quantum Systems Engineering in the United States source . The program addresses the quantum workforce gap through an interdisciplinary curriculum and industry collaboration, including a year-long, industry-sponsored capstone project and access to the Quantum Commons hub source . The first students will enroll Fall 2026, with inaugural graduates expected Spring 2029 source . The program is supported by the Elevate Quantum consortium, which includes 120 organizations source .

The Enterprise Readiness Gap

An IBM study of 2,000 executives across 33 countries and 23 industries reveals a striking disconnect: 59% believe quantum-enabled AI will transform their industry by 2030, but only 27% expect their organizations to be using quantum computing by then source . This 32-percentage-point gap indicates significant underpreparation source .

The study finds that 79% of respondents say AI will significantly contribute to revenue by 2030, but companies focused narrowly on AI risk missing the quantum shift source . Quantum computing will integrate with classical computing as complementary tools in hybrid workflows source .

Early adopters are already experimenting. Moderna uses 80-qubit systems to model mRNA secondary structures, while larger optimization problems use 156-qubit systems with 950 non-local gates source . HSBC is exploring quantum for financial optimization source .

The quantum computing market is projected to reach $72 billion by 2035 (high-end projection) or $28 billion (low-end) source . McKinsey estimates quantum computing could unlock $100 billion in value by 2035 source .

Quandela, a photonic quantum computing company, identified four key trends for 2026 : hybrid quantum-classical computing, industrial use cases, error correction, and cybersecurity source . These trends indicate quantum computing is moving from research laboratories to practical adoption source . In Canada, the quantum sector is projected to contribute $17.7 billion to GDP and generate 157,000 jobs by 2045 source .

Global Quantum Alliances

International partnerships accelerated this month. Singapore and Japan signed a Memorandum of Cooperation on quantum technology, establishing a bilateral framework with 8 priority areas source . Concurrently, Japanese hardware startup Yaqumo Inc. and Singapore-based Entropica Labs signed an MOU to collaborate on hardware-software co-design for fault-tolerant quantum computers using cold-atom systems source .

The European Photonics for Quantum (P4Q) pilot will launch in 2026 with €50 million in funding, involving 29 partners across 12 countries source . The project focuses on silicon nitride and thin-film lithium niobate photonic chips, aiming to improve reliability and scalability for quantum applications source .

PsiQuantum and Airbus announced a partnership to develop fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for aerospace applications, focusing on computational fluid dynamics source . They co-authored a technical paper presenting a Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Algorithm validated for aircraft aerodynamics, utilizing PsiQuantum’s Construct software suite source .

Quobly and TNO partnered to optimize silicon spin qubit manufacturing , focusing on bridging device engineering and materials science to improve yield and performance source .

Horizon Quantum Computing and Alice & Bob announced a strategic collaboration to accelerate fault-tolerant quantum computing software development source . The partnership integrates Alice & Bob’s quantum emulators with Horizon’s Triple Alpha development platform source .

IQM Quantum Computers and Bechtle will install a five-qubit Spark quantum computer at Heilbronn University of Applied Sciences in Germany later this year source . Bechtle will provide operational support and maintenance for the first three years source .

Ohio Representative Heidi Workman introduced House Bill 650 to establish the Frontier Technologies and Quantum Computing Commission source . The bipartisan commission will study emerging technologies including AI, quantum computing, and biotechnology to inform policy and position Ohio as a leader in innovation source .

The European Quantum Act, set for adoption in 2026, aims to align investment, governance, security, and deployment of quantum technologies to strengthen Europe’s sovereignty and competitiveness source . The policy initiative seeks to bridge gaps in patents and private capital while integrating cryptographic protections like post-quantum cryptography source .

Looking Ahead

The developments of January 2026 reveal quantum computing at a crossroads. The security awakening—marked by the “Year of Quantum Security” designation, Ethereum’s urgent response, and growing investor anxiety—signals that quantum is being taken seriously as infrastructure source . The technical advances in error correction (Alice & Bob’s 10,000x improvement, EdenCode’s real-time AI decoding) and hardware scaling (Columbia’s 360,000 optical tweezers, Russia’s 72-qubit prototype) show the field is solving real engineering challenges source .

The funding momentum (Equal1’s $60M, Photonic’s $130M) reflects investor confidence in specific technical approaches, particularly silicon-based systems compatible with existing semiconductor manufacturing source . The open-source initiative (Open Quantum Design) and workforce development efforts (Colorado School of Mines degree) address the democratization and talent pipeline challenges source .

This week marked a turning point in quantum chemistry: AI isn’t just helping us understand quantum systems anymore - it’s actively designing them. From molecules generated in 100 steps instead of 1000, to LLMs autonomously running quantum simulations, the convergence of artificial and quantum intelligence is reshaping how we discover drugs and materials.

The AI Acceleration: Designing Molecules 10x Faster

The traditional approach to molecular design has been a computational bottleneck: generate random structures, test their properties, repeat thousands of times. This week, researchers flipped the script entirely.

From Random Search to Targeted Design

PropMolFlow, a new generative AI method from the University of Florida and New York University, generates molecules 10 times faster than existing approaches while maintaining 90% chemical validity . The breakthrough lies in its “backward design” approach: instead of randomly generating molecules and checking if they have desired properties, PropMolFlow uses flow matching - a technique that creates smooth paths through chemical space - to generate structures that already target specific properties.

The efficiency gains are dramatic. Where previous diffusion-based methods required 1,000 computational steps to generate a molecule, PropMolFlow needs only 100 steps . More importantly, the method validates its results with physics-based density functional theory calculations, ensuring the generated molecules aren’t just chemically valid but physically realistic. Published in Nature Computational Science , the work integrates five different property embedding methods, making it adaptable to diverse drug discovery and materials design challenges.

“This is about solving inverse problems efficiently,” explains Stefano Martiniani, assistant professor at NYU. Rather than asking “what properties does this molecule have?”, the system asks “what molecule has these properties?” - and answers in a fraction of the time.

Collective Intelligence for Chemistry

Speed isn’t the only way AI is transforming molecular design. MOSAIC, an open-source platform from Yale University and Boehringer Ingelheim, takes a radically different approach: instead of one large AI model, it deploys 2,498 individual AI “experts” , each specialized in specific chemical reactions or synthesis techniques.

The collective intelligence approach outperforms single large language models because chemistry isn’t a monolithic domain - it’s thousands of specialized techniques, each with its own nuances. MOSAIC’s experts collaborate to generate complete experimental protocols, transforming vast chemical knowledge into actionable lab procedures. The results speak for themselves: the platform has already synthesized 35 previously unreported compounds .

The story emerging from these advances is clear: AI is moving from analysis to active design. It’s no longer just predicting properties of molecules we already know - it’s creating entirely new ones, faster and more efficiently than ever before.

LLMs Enter the Lab: Autonomous Quantum Simulation

While AI accelerates molecular design, another breakthrough is democratizing access to quantum simulation itself - traditionally a domain requiring years of specialist training.

90% Accuracy Without Years of Training

Researchers from Beijing Normal University and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology demonstrated that large language model agents can autonomously conduct tensor network simulations with 90% accuracy . Tensor networks are powerful mathematical tools for simulating quantum systems, but they’ve been notoriously difficult to use - requiring deep expertise in quantum physics, numerical methods, and specialized software packages.

The LLM-based system bypasses this barrier through in-context learning. The researchers embedded 43,000 tokens of curated documentation from the Renormalizer tensor network package directly into the system prompt, including Jupyter notebook tutorials, Python examples, and refactored source code. A multi-agent architecture then coordinates specialized agents - one for planning, one for coding, one for debugging - to autonomously set up and run quantum simulations.

The implications are profound. What once required years of training can now be accomplished by researchers with domain knowledge but no tensor network expertise. The system doesn’t replace human insight - it amplifies it, handling the technical complexity while researchers focus on the physics.

Meanwhile, quantum machine learning itself is maturing. A new chapter by Insilico Medicine scientists details how QML is transitioning from theory to targeted drug discovery applications . The work outlines practical applications across molecular representation, optimization, and generative design within hybrid quantum-classical workflows, acknowledging current limitations like hardware constraints and barren plateaus while positioning QML as a complement to classical methods rather than a replacement.

Open-Source Tools for the Quantum Era

The democratization trend extends to infrastructure. Microsoft released an updated, open-source Quantum Development Kit focused on fault-tolerant applications and molecular modeling. The QDK for Chemistry module includes AI-assisted tools for Hamiltonian generation, active space selection, and molecular visualization - and it delivers dramatic efficiency gains.

For specific molecular modeling problems, the QDK reduces gate counts from thousands to single digits . This isn’t just an incremental improvement - it’s the difference between problems that are intractable on near-term hardware and those that might run today. The toolkit integrates with VS Code, GitHub Copilot, and major quantum frameworks like Qiskit and Cirq, making it accessible to developers already familiar with classical tools.

Microsoft is also co-developing the Magne system with Atom Computing, with technical benchmarks scheduled for release on January 26, 2026. The full error correction suite is expected in late 2026.

Experimental Breakthroughs: New Pathways to Quantum Materials

While AI accelerates computation, experimental advances are making quantum materials engineering more practical. This week brought four fundamental breakthroughs that expand what’s possible.

A Shortcut to Quantum Materials

Floquet engineering - using periodic light pulses to temporarily modify material properties - has been limited by a harsh reality: it requires intense laser light that damages samples and takes tens of hours to collect data. Researchers from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology and Stanford University discovered a shortcut.

Instead of using light directly, they use excitons - bound electron-hole pairs that form when light is absorbed. Excitons couple more strongly with materials, requiring more than an order of magnitude less light intensity than optical methods. The practical impact is immediate: data acquisition time dropped from tens of hours to around two hours .

“This opens a new pathway for designing quantum materials on demand,” explains Keshav Dani, professor at OIST. The reduced energy requirements mean less sample damage, faster experiments, and access to material states that were previously too fragile to study.

Quantum Superposition at Unprecedented Scale

How large can an object be and still exhibit quantum behavior? A team pushed that boundary dramatically, demonstrating quantum interference with sodium nanoparticles containing over 7,000 atoms and masses exceeding 170,000 Da.

Using a Talbot-Lau matter-wave interferometer, the researchers showed these massive particles in quantum superposition - simultaneously taking multiple paths through space. The experiment achieved a macroscopicity measure of μ=15.5 , surpassing previous experiments by an order of magnitude. Published in Nature, the work provides the most stringent test to date of theories proposing modifications to quantum mechanics at macroscopic scales - and standard quantum theory passed with flying colors.

The de Broglie wavelength of these nanoparticles? Just 10-22 femtometers - far smaller than an atomic nucleus, yet still producing measurable interference patterns. It’s a testament to both quantum mechanics’ reach and experimental precision.

Spin Size Flips Quantum Behavior

Not all quantum boundaries are about size. A team from Osaka Metropolitan University discovered that the Kondo effect - a key quantum phenomenon where magnetic impurities interact with conduction electrons - behaves fundamentally differently depending on quantum spin size.

Using a custom-designed organic-inorganic hybrid material, they showed that spin-1/2 systems form non-magnetic singlets, while spin-1 systems promote magnetic order . This overturns the traditional view that the Kondo effect always suppresses magnetism. The discovery solves a 50-year experimental challenge in realizing the Kondo necklace model, first proposed in 1977.

The practical implication: spin size is a design knob for quantum materials. Want to suppress magnetism? Use spin-1/2. Want to enhance it? Use spin-1. It’s a new principle for engineering quantum states in materials.

Watching Electrons Break Bonds in Real Time

Finally, researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University achieved something chemists have long dreamed of: direct imaging of electrons in motion during chemical bond breaking .

Using ultrafast electron diffraction with charge pair distribution function analysis, they visualized electron and atomic nucleus dynamics as an ammonia molecule dissociated. Previous techniques could track nuclei or infer electron behavior, but this is the first direct observation of electronic activity during a chemical reaction.

The technique opens a new window into quantum chemistry. Instead of inferring reaction mechanisms from before-and-after snapshots, researchers can now watch the quantum electronic dance that governs chemical transformations. It’s a tool for testing quantum theory in real chemical systems and understanding energy transfer at the most fundamental level.

Building the Quantum-Classical Bridge

The convergence of AI and quantum chemistry requires infrastructure that seamlessly integrates quantum processors with classical supercomputers. This week brought major announcements on that front.

Nvidia detailed its NVQLink interconnect and CUDA-Q software platform, designed to tightly couple quantum processing units with GPU-accelerated supercomputers. The performance gains are striking: in a quantum chemistry workflow, GPU post-processing enabled a 656x speedup in time-to-solution. Dozens of quantum companies have signed up for NVQLink integration, with hardware shipping late 2026.

The platform focuses on three initial applications: quantum error correction, AI-driven calibration, and hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. By handling the classical pre- and post-processing on GPUs while quantum processors tackle the quantum-native parts, the system plays to each architecture’s strengths.

Microsoft’s open-source QDK, mentioned earlier, complements this hardware push with software tools. The combination of accessible development environments and high-performance interconnects is creating an ecosystem where quantum chemistry applications can move from research code to production workflows.

On the industry side, Quantumzyme Corp. announced a partnership with Predictive Research Inc. to explore AI-enabled enzyme engineering and green chemistry. The collaboration combines Quantumzyme’s computational enzyme design expertise with Predictive Research’s AI and data analytics capabilities, targeting more sustainable industrial and pharmaceutical processes.

The Convergence Ahead

Connect the dots across this week’s developments, and a clear picture emerges: we’re entering a new era where quantum chemistry becomes a practical, AI-accelerated engineering discipline rather than a purely theoretical pursuit.

AI is accelerating both the design side - PropMolFlow generating molecules 10x faster, MOSAIC coordinating thousands of synthesis experts - and the simulation side - LLM agents achieving 90% accuracy in autonomous quantum simulations, quantum machine learning moving into targeted drug discovery. Experimental advances are making quantum materials more accessible, from exciton-based Floquet engineering to real-time electron imaging. And infrastructure is being built to integrate quantum and classical computing at scale.

The convergence of these trends suggests a question worth watching: when will the first AI-designed, quantum-simulated molecule enter clinical trials? With the tools released this week, that timeline just got shorter.

The barriers to entry are falling. Open-source platforms like MOSAIC and Microsoft’s QDK mean researchers don’t need proprietary software or years of specialist training. LLM agents can handle the technical complexity of tensor network simulations. And hardware partnerships like Nvidia’s NVQLink are creating the infrastructure to run these workflows at scale.

What was once the domain of a few elite research groups is becoming accessible to anyone with domain knowledge and computational resources. That democratization, more than any single technical breakthrough, may be this week’s most significant development.

AI Systems Learn to Collaborate

A joint research team from NIMS and the University of Tsukuba developed autonomous AI network technology that enables multiple AI systems to spontaneously collaborate by sharing knowledge for materials discovery. In simulations, three AI systems exchanged knowledge and improved optimization speed through this spontaneous collaboration.

The technology mimics how human researchers communicate and share insights across labs. Rather than working in isolation, the AI systems transfer learned knowledge to each other, accelerating the exploration of materials space. The team published their findings in npj Computational Materials in December 2025.

This approach addresses a key bottleneck in computational materials discovery: each AI system typically starts from scratch, even when similar problems have been solved elsewhere. By enabling knowledge transfer between autonomous systems, the technology could accelerate the discovery and synthesis of new materials across distributed research networks.

Materials Breakthroughs

Rare-Earth-Free Magnets

Researchers at Georgetown University discovered a new class of strong magnets based on high-entropy borides that use only earth-abundant transition metals and boron. The materials exhibit high magnetic anisotropy , a key property for permanent magnets, without requiring rare-earth elements.

The team synthesized the materials using a combinatorial sputtering method that enables rapid testing of multiple compositions simultaneously—up to 50 samples on a single substrate. The high-entropy approach combines five or more elements in near-equal proportions, creating materials with properties distinct from conventional alloys.

This work opens pathways toward sustainable magnetic technologies for motors, MRI machines, and data storage. The research was published in Advanced Materials in 2025.

Robust Crystalline Sponge

The Institute of Science Tokyo developed APF-80 , a robust metal-organic framework (MOF) for the crystalline sponge method used in molecular structure analysis. Previous MOFs were too fragile for practical use, limiting the technique’s application.

APF-80 overcomes these fragility issues , enabling structural elucidation of complex, reactive molecules like alkaloids from minute quantities. The method works by absorbing target molecules into the MOF’s pores, where they can be analyzed via X-ray diffraction without requiring crystallization of the molecule itself.

This advancement is expected to accelerate pharmaceutical research by enabling structure determination of compounds that are difficult to crystallize or available only in small amounts.

New Quantum State

Physicists from Rice University and Vienna University of Technology discovered a topological semimetal phase in CeRu4Sn6 at near absolute zero temperature. The state emerged through quantum criticality and was identified via an unusual Hall effect without an external magnetic field.

The finding challenges previous assumptions: strong electron interactions can create, not destroy, topological states . This insight could inform advances in quantum computing, electronic efficiencies, and sensing technologies by revealing new mechanisms for engineering topological quantum materials.

Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Chicago developed an AI advisor model for autonomous labs that enables collaborative decision-making between humans and AI. The work provides experimental evidence for quantum advantage in materials discovery, particularly when working with complex diffraction data and limited experimental samples . The findings suggest quantum computing could accelerate autonomous experimentation in materials science.

Data Infrastructure

NIMS developed Research Data Express (RDE) , a flexible data management system designed to standardize and automate materials science data processing. Since its 2023 launch, the platform has seen significant adoption: 5,000 users , 1,900 Dataset Templates implemented, 16,000 datasets created, and 3 million accumulated data files .

RDE uses customizable Dataset Templates to interpret data from various experiments, reducing researchers’ data processing burden and promoting FAIR data principles. The system serves as key infrastructure for Japan’s national materials science initiatives, addressing the critical bottleneck of inconsistent and siloed data that hampers collaborative research and AI-driven discovery.

Energy Fuels is acquiring Australian Strategic Materials for approximately $447 million AUD, highlighting strategic moves to secure critical minerals supply chains and reduce dependence on China for rare earth processing.

Also This Week

Pablo Jarillo-Herrero (MIT) and Allan MacDonald (University of Texas) won the BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Award for their discovery of the “magic angle” in graphene layers. Their work on twistronics—rotating graphene at 1.1 degrees to control electronic properties—has applications in quantum computing and energy-efficient AI.

D-Wave Creates First Dual-Platform Quantum Company

D-Wave finalized its $550 million acquisition of Quantum Circuits Inc., positioning itself as the only company offering both annealing and gate-model quantum computing systems. The deal, structured as $300 million in stock and $250 million in cash , brings together two distinct approaches to quantum computing: annealing systems excel at optimization problems, while gate-model systems are general-purpose quantum computers suitable for a wider range of algorithms.

The acquisition gives D-Wave access to Quantum Circuits’ dual-rail qubit technology , which reduces the physical qubit overhead for fault-tolerant systems by up to 200 times. This error-detecting architecture uses two physical modes to represent quantum information, offering built-in error detection that could significantly accelerate the path to practical quantum computing.

D-Wave plans to release a 49-qubit gate-model system in 2026 , complementing its existing Advantage annealing platform. The company will establish a new R&D center in New Haven, Connecticut, and Dr. Rob Schoelkopf , Quantum Circuits’ co-founder and Yale professor, joins as Chief Scientist.

Technical Breakthroughs

IBM Demonstrates Reliable Quantum Simulations

IBM researchers used a 91-qubit superconducting processor to accurately reproduce signatures of quantum chaos, demonstrating that current noisy quantum computers can provide reliable scientific insights before fault-tolerant machines arrive. The study, published in Nature, executed 4,000 two-qubit gates using dual-unitary circuits designed to benchmark complex many-body physics.

The key to achieving reliable results was tensor-network error mitigation (TEM) , an advanced technique that reduces the impact of noise on quantum computations without requiring full error correction. The researchers tested system sizes ranging from 51 to 91 qubits and completed the entire workflow in 3 hours , demonstrating practical near-term quantum utility.

The work shows that error-mitigated quantum simulation can adjudicate between conflicting classical methods for complex physics problems, providing a credible path for scientific value from pre-fault-tolerant quantum computers.

Alice & Bob’s Error Correction Advance

Alice & Bob unveiled “Elevator Codes,” a novel error correction method for its cat qubit quantum computers that promises a 10,000x lower logical error rate while requiring only about 3x more qubits compared to its current error correction approach.

The technique uses code concatenation to make a logical ancilla qubit operate like an elevator within repetition codes, enabling detection of bit-flips at the logical level. Cat qubits already suppress phase-flip errors through their biased noise characteristics, and Elevator Codes address the remaining bit-flip errors with remarkable efficiency. This advancement could dramatically reduce the overhead of error correction, making large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computations more attainable.

Open-Source Quantum Computing Initiative

The University of Waterloo launched Open Quantum Design (OQD) , a non-profit organization hosting the world’s first open-source, full-stack quantum computer using trapped-ion technology. The initiative has attracted 30 software contributors and aims to accelerate progress by providing open access to hardware and software for algorithm testing and workforce training.

OQD represents a collaborative third path distinct from traditional academic labs and commercial startups, with partners including Haiqu and Xanadu. The project builds on eight years of computing hardware development at the Institute for Quantum Computing.

Security Vulnerabilities Identified

Penn State researchers warned about security flaws in quantum computers themselves, highlighting vulnerabilities in both software and hardware. The study identified issues including crosstalk and lack of program integrity verification that could make quantum systems targets for cyberattacks. The researchers urge developers to safeguard quantum systems from the ground up as the technology moves toward wider use.

Quantum Threats to Cryptocurrency

The cryptocurrency industry is grappling with quantum computing’s potential threat to cryptographic security. Jefferies, a global investment banking firm, removed its 10% Bitcoin allocation from its model portfolio, with strategist Christopher Wood citing quantum computing as a potential threat to Bitcoin’s cryptographic foundations. The allocation was shifted to physical gold and gold mining stocks.

Coinbase responded by forming an Independent Advisory Board on Quantum Computing and Blockchain , bringing together experts including quantum computing pioneer Scott Aaronson, Stanford cryptography expert Dan Boneh, and Ethereum researcher Justin Drake. The board will assess risks, publish position papers, and recommend best practices, with its first paper expected in early 2027.

Meanwhile, quantum-software firm BlueQubit launched a public challenge offering 0.25 BTC ($22,500) to anyone who can solve a cryptographic problem. The company claims its quantum computer can find the hidden private key in under two hours, while classical supercomputers would take years.

Market Activity

Rigetti Computing secured an $8.4 million order from India’s Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) for a 108-qubit quantum computer . The system will be installed on-premises in Bengaluru with deployment scheduled for H2 2026 , building on an existing partnership and highlighting growing demand for on-premises quantum computers.

Montana State University’s QCORE received a $31.5 million contract from the Air Force Research Laboratory to advance quantum infrastructure. The funding will expand quantum networking test beds, integrate advanced sensors and computing architectures, and accelerate commercialization of quantum technologies. This builds on a prior $26.7 million grant awarded in 2023.

Chinese quantum computing company SpinQ Technology closed a Series C funding round , raising hundreds of millions of RMB (roughly $14-40 million USD) led by Longli Technology and Jadex Capital. The funds will advance the company’s full-stack quantum systems and expand its global footprint.

Irish startup Equal1 raised $60 million to scale its silicon-based quantum computing systems. The funding will accelerate rollout of its Bell-1 quantum server and scale manufacturing using existing semiconductor foundries, focusing on standard CMOS fabrication to lower cost and deployment barriers.

Microsoft released an updated open-source Quantum Development Kit that streamlines fault-tolerant quantum application development. The kit includes specialized tools for chemistry modeling and error correction, with AI-assisted coding and support for multiple quantum frameworks including Q#, OpenQASM, Qiskit, and Cirq.

Policy and Infrastructure

Rep. Chuck Fleischmann of Tennessee advocated for increased federal investment in quantum computing, AI, and supercomputing, arguing they are critical for U.S. national security and global leadership. The congressman warned that adversaries like China are heavily investing in these technologies and positioned Tennessee to play a leading role through involvement with the Department of Energy and all 17 national lab directors.

Ohio State Representative Heidi Workman introduced House Bill 650 to establish the Frontier Technologies and Quantum Computing Commission. The bipartisan commission will study emerging technologies like AI, quantum computing, and biotechnology to inform policy and position Ohio as an innovation leader while addressing economic, ethical, and security implications.

Europe launched the $50 million Photonics for Quantum (P4Q) pilot line to industrialize quantum photonic chips. The project, coordinated by the University of Twente with 29 partners across 12 countries, aims to develop standardized production techniques for photonic chips used in quantum computing, sensing, and secure communication.

What to Watch

This week’s developments reflect steady progress across multiple fronts. D-Wave’s dual-platform strategy signals industry maturation, with companies recognizing that different quantum computing approaches serve different applications. The acquisition brings together optimization-focused annealing systems with general-purpose gate-model computing, creating a more comprehensive offering for customers.

Error correction and mitigation techniques continue advancing, with IBM demonstrating practical near-term utility through tensor-network error mitigation and Alice & Bob achieving dramatic efficiency gains with Elevator Codes. These advances show progress toward practical systems without requiring full fault-tolerant quantum computers.

The cryptocurrency debate highlights real-world security concerns as quantum computing capabilities grow. While the timeline for quantum threats to current cryptography remains uncertain, the industry response—from Jefferies’ portfolio adjustment to Coinbase’s advisory board—demonstrates increasing awareness and preparation.

Geographic spread of activity is notable, with significant developments in India (Rigetti’s $8.4M order), China (SpinQ’s Series C), Europe (€50M photonics pilot line), and the United States (Montana State’s $31.5M contract). This international competition is driving both investment and policy attention.

Key milestones ahead include D-Wave’s 49-qubit gate-model system in 2026, Rigetti’s India deployment in H2 2026, and Microsoft’s full error correction suite expected in late 2026. These concrete deliverables will test whether the industry can transition from research demonstrations to commercial deployment.
