The Big Story: AI Goes Physical

The most significant infrastructure investment in AI materials discovery to date comes from Google DeepMind, which is building its first automated research laboratory for material discovery in the United Kingdom. Scheduled to be operational by 2026 , the facility will combine Gemini AI with advanced robotics to synthesize and analyze hundreds of material samples daily targeting applications like superconductors, high-performance batteries, solar cells, chips, and medical imaging.

The lab is part of a broader partnership with the UK government that includes sharing AI models with the UK AI Security Institute and providing British researchers priority access to AI systems. Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, announced the initiative in December 2025, alongside UK Technology Secretary Liz Kendall. Google has separately committed £5 billion ($6.3 billion) to data-center and operational investments in the UK over the next two years.

This UK facility is one component of a larger strategy. Google DeepMind is also partnering with the U.S. Department of Energy as part of the White House’s Genesis Mission a national effort to use AI to accelerate scientific research. Through this partnership, Google will provide all 17 DOE National Laboratories with access to its frontier AI models and tools, starting with the AI co-scientist built on Gemini. The collaboration aims to accelerate breakthroughs in energy, materials discovery, and national security, with an accelerated access program expanding to National Laboratories in early 2026 .

Despite these major infrastructure investments, the field has yet to produce a major commercial breakthrough. As MIT Technology Review notes in its analysis , AI-driven materials discovery is moving from computational simulation to real-world experimentation, but the critical bottleneck remains physically making and testing predicted compounds. The typical timeline to develop and manufacture a new material still spans 20 years and no AI-discovered material has yet achieved commercial scale.

Bridging the Prediction-Reality Gap

The fundamental challenge in AI materials discovery is no longer prediction, it is physical synthesis and testing. The field is developing multiple approaches to bridge this gap.

Startup Approaches

Venture-backed startups are building autonomous labs where AI agents design and run experiments to synthesize and optimize new materials. Lila Sciences, co-founded by Rafael Gómez-Bombarelli (MIT professor of materials science) with chief autonomous science officer John Gregoire, has raised hundreds of millions of dollars to pursue this approach. Periodic Labs, co-founded by physicist Ekin Dogus Cubuk and Liam Fedus (co-creator of ChatGPT), is building similar facilities focused on automated experimentation.

These startups aim to drastically shorten the decades-long development timeline for new materials needed for batteries, carbon capture, and next-generation computing. Their autonomous labs use techniques like sputtering for materials deposition, with AI agents conducting experiments at scales impractical for human researchers.

Human-in-the-Loop Systems

Rather than full automation, some researchers are finding success with collaborative human-AI frameworks. Scientists from Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering developed an AI advisor model that enables shared control in self-driving labs. Applied to electronic materials, specifically mixed ion-electron conducting polymers (MIECPs), the system achieved a 150% performance improvement over previous cutting-edge techniques.

The research, published in Nature Chemical Engineering, introduces an adaptive AI decision interface for autonomous experimentation that enables real-time human-AI collaboration. The platform successfully optimized conducting polymers in just 64 autonomous trials , achieving a mixed-conducting figure of merit (\(\mu C^*\)) ranging from 166 to 1,275 F cm\(^{-1}\) V\(^{-1}\) s\(^{-1}\) . The work also uncovered a previously unknown polymer polymorph , demonstrating the platform’s potential for accelerated materials discovery through adaptive experimentation that combines AI data analysis with human decision-making.

Concrete Discoveries

While much of the focus is on methodology, AI is also producing tangible materials discoveries.

Magnetic Sensors

Researchers at the National Institute for Materials Science (NIMS) developed a high-throughput experimental method that measures anomalous Hall resistivity 30 times faster than conventional techniques. Combining this method with machine learning, they discovered a new ternary magnetic sensor material (Fe-Ir-Pt) with a record-high anomalous Hall resistivity of 6.5 \(\mu\Omega \cdot cm\) significantly exceeding the previous maximum of 5.25 \(\mu\Omega \cdot cm\) in Fe-X binary systems.

The new method reduces evaluation time per composition to 0.2 hours (12 minutes) , enabling rapid screening of compositional gradient thin films. This data-driven pipeline accelerates the search for sensitive magnetic sensor materials crucial for next-generation hard disk drives, published in npj Computational Materials.

Superconductors

Tohoku University and Fujitsu Limited used the Fujitsu Kozuchi AI platform to analyze the superconductivity mechanism of a kagome superconducting material, cesium vanadium antimonide (CsV\(_3\)Sb\(_5\)). Their new discovery intelligence technique compressed causal graphs derived from complex experimental data to 1/20th of their original size , enabling efficient identification of the material’s electron interactions.

The research leverages data from the NanoTerasu Synchrotron Light Source (operational since April 2024) and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). Fujitsu plans to begin offering a trial environment for the discovery intelligence technology in March 2026 , following the 2022 establishment of the Fujitsu x Tohoku University Discovery Intelligence Laboratory.

LLM-Powered Discovery

Researchers at the University of Tokyo developed MatAgent, an AI framework using large language models for autonomous and explainable materials discovery. The system reasons step-by-step in natural language , explains its decisions, and incorporates user constraints to efficiently search for new inorganic materials. Published in Cell Reports Physical Science, the approach aims to accelerate discovery of materials for catalysis, energy storage, and semiconductors by making AI-driven discovery more transparent and explainable.

Other Discoveries

  • Topological materials: Researchers from the University of Alabama at Birmingham and Shenzhen University developed a quantum-inspired chemical rule using a hybrid quantum-classical artificial neural network to predict topological materials from chemical composition, achieving 84.7% prediction accuracy and successfully identifying new topological compounds.

  • Ultralow thermal conductivity: A study in Nature Communications introduced a universal descriptor for thermal conductivity based on atomic number and sound velocity, enabling fast screening of materials. Using high-throughput workflows and machine learning, researchers identified candidates from over 25,000 materials and experimentally validated record-low thermal conductivity in CsAg\(_2\)I\(_3\).

The Reality Check

As the field scales up, researchers are identifying specific technical limitations that AI-based materials prediction must overcome.

The Crystallographic Disorder Problem

An international study led by the University of Bayreuth, Fritz Haber Institute, and Imperial College London reveals that AI and computer simulations often make significant errors in predicting material properties because they ignore crystallographic disorder a common feature in real-world crystals. The researchers developed a machine-learning tool to detect disordered materials and found that in one database, over 80% of AI-predicted promising materials were likely affected by disorder that simulations missed.

The tool, published in Advanced Materials, addresses substitutional disorder a phenomenon where multiple elements randomly occupy crystallographic sites. Prof. Dr. Johannes T. Margraf (University of Bayreuth) and first author Konstantin Jakob (Fritz Haber Institute) present the detection tool as a way to improve reliability and efficiency of computer-assisted material discovery, preventing costly experimental failures based on flawed predictions.

Acknowledging Limitations

MIT Technology Review examines the gap between promise and reality , noting that while Google’s DeepMind has predicted millions of new materials, only hundreds have actually been made in the lab . The publication characterizes the field as still in early stages and prone to hype, with significant challenges in translating AI predictions into novel, useful, and physically viable materials.

Similarly, Semiconductor Engineering reviews the benefits and limits of machine learning for materials discovery. While ML tools enable a 100-fold reduction in candidates for synthesis, the analysis emphasizes that these tools rely heavily on human expertise for data preparation, validation, and interpretation to overcome limitations like selection bias and model explainability. Case studies from IBM, Microsoft Research, and Samsung demonstrate that ML integration with human judgment is essential for reliable outcomes.

Methodological Advances

Beyond applications, researchers are developing new computational and experimental frameworks for AI-accelerated materials science.

Computational Methods

A review in Nature Computational Materials discusses how machine learning and quantum computing can accelerate discovery of high-entropy materials for energy applications like batteries and supercapacitors. The work focuses on overcoming data and modeling obstacles to predict material properties before physical synthesis, highlighting the potential of high-entropy MXenes to overcome limitations of conventional battery materials.

Researchers from the University of Manchester are using AI to accelerate quantum materials discovery, with an AI system that “learns to think like a physicist” to predict promising materials and guide their fabrication. Led by Dr. Qian Yang (Royal Society University Research Fellow at the National Graphene Institute), the work aims to underpin breakthroughs in lossless superconductors and clean energy catalysts.

Experimental Integration

A study in Nature Computational Materials presents an Active Learning loop implementation in pyiron for experimental materials characterization, combining experimental and simulated data. The approach uses prior knowledge from density functional theory simulations and text mining to accelerate characterization, drawing inspiration from high-throughput simulation workflows to bridge computation and experiment.

Researchers propose a framework for networking autonomous material exploration systems using transfer learning to share knowledge and improve discovery efficiency. Demonstrated with three distinct systems targeting different material properties, the approach uses ensemble neural networks and Bayesian optimization to enable large-scale autonomous networks that could accelerate material development through knowledge exchange.

Quantum Applications

A research team including scientists from General Motors demonstrates that quantum algorithms can accurately simulate transition metal oxides used in automotive catalysts. Their resource estimation shows simulating a key catalyst fragment to chemical accuracy could require 300 to 10 million physical qubits , a scale projected for future hardware. Led by Yuntao Gu, Louis Hector, Jr, and Paolo Giusto from GM, the work validates applying quantum computing to real-world materials science and provides a roadmap for near-term simulations of catalytic materials.

Funding and Ecosystem

Startup activity continues in the materials discovery space. Novyte Materials raised INR 4.15 crore (approximately $50,000) in a pre-seed round led by Theia Ventures. The startup uses generative AI and physics-based simulations to compress R&D timelines by 10 times and reduce early-stage physical testing costs by 90% . The funding represents Theia Ventures’ fourth investment from its new fund, which announced its first close in October 2025.

While modest compared to the hundreds of millions raised by Lila Sciences, the investment shows continued startup activity in AI-driven materials discovery despite the field’s lack of commercial breakthroughs.

Looking Ahead

The developments of December 2025 reveal a field in transition. Google DeepMind’s automated lab represents a major bet that physical experimentation at scale is the path forward. The human-AI collaboration work suggests pure automation isn’t the only answer hybrid approaches that combine AI’s analytical capabilities with human judgment may prove more effective. The crystallographic disorder study reveals specific, addressable technical challenges that must be overcome for AI predictions to translate reliably to real materials.

The lack of commercial breakthroughs, as noted by MIT Technology Review, suggests the field is still in early days despite the hype and investment. AI may accelerate discovery from decades to years, not months. The realistic timeline for AI-discovered materials to reach commercial application remains measured in years, not months.

Approach Key Example Status
Fully Automated Labs Google DeepMind UK facility Opening 2026
Human-AI Collaboration AI advisor at Argonne 150% performance gain demonstrated
Startup Labs Lila Sciences, Periodic Labs Early stage, no major breakthroughs

As 2026 approaches, the key question for the field is: Will physical validation match the computational promise? The Google DeepMind lab, scheduled to open next year, will be a critical test case. Success would validate the large-scale investment in automated experimentation. Continued challenges would reinforce the value of hybrid human-AI approaches and highlight the need for continued fundamental research into the complexities of real-world materials.

The field is growing up identifying specific problems like crystallographic disorder, developing concrete solutions like disorder-detection ML tools, and building infrastructure like the UK automated lab. This maturation from hype to measured progress may be the most important development of all.

This comprehensive review covers 65 articles published during December 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing. As the field matures from hype toward measurable progress, researchers proposed standardized KPIs to evaluate quantum systems, silicon-based chips demonstrated record fidelities, and error correction crossed new thresholds globally.

The Big Story: Quantum Computing Seeks Standard Metrics

As quantum computing matures, the field is grappling with a fundamental problem: how to objectively measure progress. In December, researchers proposed key performance indicators (KPIs) to standardize the evaluation of quantum systems, aiming to distinguish genuine breakthroughs from spurious claims. The effort, documented in a 2025 preprint by Lall et al., seeks to provide comparable metrics across different hardware platforms, algorithms, and evaluation methods.

The push for standardization comes as the field grapples with what metrics actually matter. Research published in Nature Communications and elsewhere has shown that stabilizer metrics may only provide an upper bound on quantum performance, not a complete picture of system capability. Meanwhile, researchers have mapped how errors evolve over time in quantum memory systems, providing better context for what reliability claims mean in practice.

Concrete verification methods are also emerging. Scientists at Swinburne University developed techniques to verify the accuracy of Gaussian Boson Sampler (GBS) devices, quickly identifying errors in experiments that would take thousands of years to simulate classically. The method can detect deviations from expected results, a critical capability as quantum systems grow too complex for classical verification.

This focus on measurement reflects a broader shift in the field. As McKinsey noted in a December analysis , quantum leaders and investors are increasingly prioritizing quantum error correction as the critical path to utility, with investment in quantum startups surging 50% in 2024.

Error Correction Breakthroughs

Microwave Control Advances

Chinese researchers achieved a significant milestone in December, demonstrating fault-tolerant quantum error correction using an all-microwave method on a 107-qubit processor. This marks the first time a group outside the US has crossed this key reliability threshold. The team, led by Pan Jianwei from the University of Science and Technology of China, achieved an error-suppression factor of 1.4 with a distance-7 surface-code logical qubit—a scale comparable to Google’s recent advances.

The microwave-based approach offers a practical advantage: it suppresses leakage errors without requiring extra hardware, potentially easing scaling bottlenecks. As reported in Physical Review Letters , the method tackles qubit drift and error propagation more efficiently than hardware-intensive approaches.

Complementary research from the same team demonstrated a new method to fix leakage errors using targeted microwave pulses . Tested on a 97-qubit processor, the technique suppressed leakage errors over 70 times more effectively than running without suppression. Critically, the system became more reliable as more qubits were added—a key requirement for scalable quantum computing.

Hardware Solutions

European researchers achieved a breakthrough in superconducting qubit control, developing analytical formulas called R1D and R2D that achieve gate fidelities of 99.999% for rapid X-gate rotations. The work from Forschungszentrum Jülich, University of Cologne, and RWTH Aachen University addresses limitations in qubit control under strong driving, providing a blueprint for more reliable quantum processors.

On the decoding side, Riverlane published a peer-reviewed paper in Nature Communications detailing its Local Clustering Decoder (LCD), a hardware decoder that achieves real-time quantum error correction for the surface code. The decoder breaks the traditional trade-off between speed and accuracy, performing one round in under a microsecond and adapting to changing noise conditions. It forms the core of Riverlane’s Deltaflow stack and has been deployed on systems from partners including Infleqtion and Rigetti Computing.

Silicon Chips Show Record Fidelities

Silicon Quantum Computing (SQC) published breakthrough results in Nature in December, demonstrating an 11-qubit quantum processor in silicon that achieves fidelity rates between 99.5% and 99.99% . The processor uses a novel “14/15” architecture that places phosphorus atoms in silicon with atomic precision, achieving feature sizes of just 0.13 nanometers.

The significance of this work goes beyond the numbers. As SQC’s research shows, their silicon-based processor scales without losing fidelity —qubit quality actually improves as qubit count increases, contrary to typical quantum systems. The architecture demonstrates atomic, silicon-based quantum computing across separate clusters for the first time, with multi-register linkages maintaining fidelities above fault-tolerance benchmarks.

This modular approach addresses what SQC calls the key quantum scaling problem : how to connect qubit registers while preserving high gate fidelities. The company’s proprietary atomic-scale manufacturing process, developed over 25 years, allows it to produce its own quantum chips with 0.13 nanometer precision.

On the commercialization front, SEALSQ announced a CMOS-compatible roadmap targeting quantum processor production from 2026 to 2030, positioning silicon-based approaches as a potentially manufacturable path to scale.

Capital Moves: Quantum Art $100M, Government Investments

Private Funding

Quantum Art closed a $100 million Series A funding round to scale its multi-core trapped-ion quantum computers, bringing total funding to $124 million. The round, one of the largest for trapped-ion systems, will accelerate development of the company’s 1,000-qubit Perspective system and prototyping of a third-generation architecture targeting thousands of qubits. The company also demonstrated a 200-ion chain and collaborations with NVIDIA and Ayalon Highways.

Nu Quantum raised $60 million in Series A funding , the largest financing round for quantum computer networking. The Cambridge-based company is developing quantum networking technology to enable distributed quantum computing.

QubitSolve secured a $1.2 million NSF SBIR Phase II grant to accelerate development of its quantum computational fluid dynamics (CFD) software. The Morgantown-based startup is transitioning from a 2D prototype to a 3D minimum viable product, with commercial release targeted for late 2027.

Government Investment

Canada launched the Canadian Quantum Champions Program, allocating up to $92 million in initial public funding to four domestic quantum firms—Anyon Systems, Nord Quantique, Photonic, and Xanadu Quantum Technologies. This Phase 1 initiative is part of a broader $334.3 million investment from Budget 2025 aimed at strengthening Canada’s quantum ecosystem and developing fault-tolerant quantum computers.

The Oak Ridge Quantum Science Center secured $125 million in DOE funding for its 2025-2030 program, focusing on quantum materials research and joined-up, multidisciplinary approaches to quantum challenges.

Fujitsu announced a $100,000 quantum simulator challenge , inviting researchers to tackle real-world problems using its 40-qubit quantum simulator.

Company Amount Type Focus
Quantum Art $100M Series A Trapped-ion systems
Nu Quantum $60M Series A Quantum networking
Canada Champions $92M Government 4 domestic firms
Oak Ridge QSC $125M DOE funding 2025-30 program

Global Quantum Deployments Accelerate

Europe

Spain’s CESGA selected IQM Quantum Computers and Telefónica to deploy two on-premises quantum computers: a 54-qubit IQM Radiance system and a 5-qubit IQM Spark for education. Scheduled for delivery by June 2026, this marks Spain’s first quantum-HPC integration and IQM’s first installation in the country.

In Germany, Universal Quantum and Atlas Copco partnered to co-develop industrial-grade vacuum systems for scalable trapped-ion quantum computers. The collaboration aims to transition vacuum technology from laboratory tools to integrated solutions for modular quantum architectures.

FullStaQD announced a new quantum software stack to optimize quantum application development, part of broader European efforts to build complete quantum computing ecosystems.

Qilimanjaro and Oxigen Data Center partnered on multimodal quantum-HPC integration, enabling hybrid quantum-classical workflows for Spanish researchers.

Asia-Pacific & Middle East

Israel’s Quantum Computing Center (IQCC) deployed Qolab’s scalable superconducting qubit device , marking the first installation of the Nobel laureate-founded company’s hardware outside its US lab. The device uses Quantum Machines’ control technology and will be available via cloud access.

Chile launched a National Quantum Strategy 2025-2035 , prioritizing sovereign capabilities in quantum computing, sensing, and communications. The strategy aims to transition Chile to a knowledge-based economy with applications in mining, energy, and telecommunications.

India’s Andhra Pradesh unveiled a Quantum Vision plan to establish Amaravati as a global quantum computing hub among the world’s top five. The initiative targets local quantum computer production within two years and includes a Rs 100-crore (approximately $12 million) Nobel Prize award for quantum research.

In Singapore, Keysight Technologies entered a five-year collaboration with A*STAR, NUS, and NTU to co-develop scalable qubit control architectures, integrating digital control systems with novel processor architectures.

Xanadu expanded its partnership with A*STAR to advance photonic quantum computing, strengthening Singapore’s position in the quantum landscape.

The UK’s National Quantum Computing Centre partnered with Google to give UK researchers access to Google’s advanced Willow quantum chip through an open competition, aiming to uncover new real-world applications in chemistry and medicine.

Location System Qubits Timeline Partner
Spain (CESGA) IQM Radiance 54 By June 2026 IQM, Telefónica
Israel (IQCC) Qolab Scalable Deployed Qolab, Quantum Machines
Chile National Strategy N/A 2025-2035 Government-led

Research Roundup: Optical Chips, Algorithms, and Applications

Optical Advances

Researchers developed a tiny optical phase modulator nearly 100 times smaller than a human hair that uses 80 times less microwave power than commercial modulators. The device, from University of Colorado at Boulder and Sandia National Laboratories, uses microwave-frequency vibrations to manipulate laser light and is manufactured using scalable CMOS fabrication. This breakthrough could enable control of thousands or millions of qubits for trapped-ion and trapped-neutral-atom quantum computers.

Multiple publications highlighted the significance of this work. As reported in ScienceDaily , the chip oscillates billions of times per second and is aimed at the critical bottleneck of optical control for scaling quantum computers. Stanford University researchers separately demonstrated room-temperature quantum communication using molybdenum diselenide and silicon nanostructures, potentially enabling low-cost quantum technologies without extreme cooling.

Algorithms & Software

Researchers developed CircPack, a framework for parallel execution of quantum circuits on trapped-ion computers that treats circuit scheduling as a packing problem. The framework achieves up to 70.72% higher fidelity, 62.67% better utilization, and 32.80% improved layer reduction compared to existing methods, enhancing quantum cloud computing efficiency.

Nature Communications published research on AI integration into the quantum stack, demonstrating how machine learning can optimize quantum operations.

Neutral-Atom Progress

Researchers at Xiangtan University trapped 2,400 Ytterbium-174 atoms in an optical tweezer array with 83.5% loading efficiency, a significant improvement in scalability for quantum computing. The achievement, using optimized laser cooling and real-time feedback, paves the way for larger quantum systems with estimated two-qubit gate fidelities of 99.9%.

Atom Computing developed a method for “qubit recycling” , replenishing atoms from a separate trap to reduce errors and atom loss in neutral-atom quantum computers. Published in Physical Review X, the work enables more complex and longer quantum circuits.

Russian researchers from Lomonosov Moscow State University tested a 72-qubit quantum computer based on neutral rubidium atoms, achieving 94% accuracy in two-qubit operations. The system uses a three-zone architecture for computation, storage, and readout, with plans to reach several hundred high-fidelity qubits by 2030.

Applications

Xanadu published a quantum computational framework demonstrating how fault-tolerant quantum computers can model photosensitizers for photodynamic cancer therapy. The research provides resource estimates for utility-scale hardware and projects significant runtime reductions for classical simulation bottlenecks. The announcement coincided with Xanadu’s planned business combination expected to provide approximately $500 million in capital.

Researchers from IBM, RIKEN, Google, and Quantinuum demonstrated progress in applying quantum computers to chemistry problems throughout 2025 . Qunova Computing reported a quantum algorithm achieving 10 times the efficiency of traditional methods for chemistry calculations.

Nature published research on quantum computing methods for materials simulation, expanding the range of applications for near-term quantum hardware.

Networked Systems

IonQ published a study finding that linked quantum computers can outperform larger single systems. The research suggests a modular approach to scaling rather than building monolithic processors.

Japan achieved a milestone in remote quantum computing , enabling cloud-based access to quantum systems across geographical distances.

Industry Briefs

Amazon reorganized its quantum computing efforts , combining AI, silicon, and quantum computing under a unified structure to streamline development and resource allocation.

Microsoft’s Majorana 1 quantum computer chip continued to generate discussion and controversy . The chip relies on unproven topological qubits based on Majorana zero modes, with some experts remaining unconvinced by the data. Microsoft’s project advanced to the final phase of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative.

IonQ highlighted the historical significance of Dr. Chris Monroe’s 1995 quantum logic gate , which marked the practical birth of quantum computing. The company, founded in 2015, now targets 80,000 logical qubits by 2030 and recently announced a world-record 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity.

IBM announced expansion of its Quantum program in Poughkeepsie, New York, planning to build the world’s first large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers by 2033 via its Starling (2029) and Bluejay (2033) projects. The expansion is part of IBM’s broader $1 billion investment in quantum services.

Quantum Computing Inc. agreed to acquire Luminar Semiconductor for $110 million in an all-cash transaction, bringing photonic technologies, patents, and talent to accelerate its quantum systems roadmap.

D-Wave announced it will showcase its quantum computing technology at CES 2026, highlighting real-world customer success stories and applications.

The telecom industry is preparing for quantum computing’s impact by enhancing network security with quantum-safe technologies like post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD). Companies including Orange Business, Telefónica, and Nokia are offering solutions and exploring quantum computing for network optimization.

MOTH, a quantum technology company, announced that quantum computing can overcome classical computing limits in game development, introducing Archaeo, a hardware-agnostic quantum platform for creative workflows, and highlighting Space Moths, a multiplayer game that uses quantum computers to generate levels in real time.

Looking Ahead to 2026

The developments of December 2025 point to a field maturing toward practical applications. Microsoft has introduced a three-level framework for quantum computing progress , with level-two error-corrected machines set for delivery in 2026. These machines, built by Microsoft with Atom Computing and by QuEra, use neutral atoms as qubits for improved scalability and error correction.

The partnership between Microsoft and Atom Computing will deliver the Magne machine with 50 logical qubits and 1,200 physical qubits by the start of 2027. QuEra’s machine at AIST will feature 37 logical qubits across 260 physical qubits. These systems mark the transition from NISQ-era devices to the first generation of error-corrected quantum computers.

McKinsey’s analysis emphasizes that quantum error correction is the priority for capturing value from quantum technologies, which could generate between $0.9 trillion and $2.0 trillion by 2035. The firm notes that quantum start-up investments were 50% higher in 2024 than 2023, with the market projected to reach nearly $100 billion by 2035.

Looking at 2025 investment trends, The Quantum Insider reports a shift away from broad experimentation toward more targeted bets on trapped-ion and photonic hardware architectures, cloud-accessible quantum software platforms, and quantum security technologies. Individual funding rounds for trapped-ion and photonic quantum computer companies reached the $1 billion range.

IBM’s roadmap targets fully error-corrected quantum machines by 2029 , with large-scale systems capable of 1 billion quantum operations by 2029 and 1 billion operations by 2033. The company positions the Hudson Valley as “Quantum Valley,” building on its history of mainframe computing innovation.

As the University of Oxford’s new Quantum Institute Director Ian Walmsley noted , the field is setting the agenda for the next century of quantum science, with deep expertise and cross-disciplinary collaboration accelerating impact across computing, communications, and sensing.

As NeurIPS 2025 approaches, researchers from SAKURA internet and Kyoto University will present MatPROV—a dataset that extracts material synthesis procedures from literature as structured directed graphs using large language models.

This comprehensive review covers 1 article published in November 2025, examining how natural language processing can unlock procedural knowledge trapped in scientific literature.

The Research: Structuring Synthesis Knowledge

A paper from SAKURA internet Research Center has been accepted for the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2025, introducing MatPROV—a dataset that applies large language models to the challenge of extracting material synthesis procedures from scientific literature.

The research team, led by Hirofumi Tsuruta and Masaya Kumagai from SAKURA internet (with Kumagai also affiliated with Kyoto University), will present their work on December 6, 2025, at the AI4Mat Workshop in New Orleans.

What MatPROV Does

MatPROV addresses a fundamental problem in materials science: synthesis procedures exist as unstructured text in scientific papers—paragraphs describing multi-step workflows in inconsistent formats across thousands of publications. This makes it difficult for AI systems to learn from historical data or plan new syntheses.

The MatPROV approach uses large language models (LLMs) to parse natural language descriptions of material synthesis and convert them into structured representations. Specifically, the output is a directed graph where nodes represent materials and operations, and edges capture dependencies between steps.

The PROV-DM Standard

What distinguishes MatPROV from other extraction efforts is its use of the PROV-DM (Provenance Data Model) standard. PROV-DM is a W3C recommendation for representing provenance information—the lineage of entities, activities, and agents involved in producing a piece of data.

In the context of materials synthesis, PROV-DM provides a formal way to represent:

  • Entities: The materials, reagents, and equipment involved
  • Activities: The processing steps, reactions, and transformations
  • Agents: The researchers, instruments, or automated systems performing actions
  • Derivations: How output materials derive from input materials

This standardized representation enables computational analysis, similarity search between procedures, and integration with laboratory automation systems.

Component Description
Input Unstructured synthesis procedures from scientific literature
Extraction Method Large language models (LLMs) parse natural language text
Data Standard PROV-DM (W3C Provenance Data Model)
Output Format Structured directed graphs (nodes: materials/operations, edges: dependencies)
Application Electronic laboratory notebooks, AI-driven synthesis planning

Research Team and Affiliations

The paper comes from SAKURA internet Inc., a Japanese internet infrastructure company that has established a research center working at the intersection of cloud computing and materials informatics. The dual affiliation of Masaya Kumagai—SAKURA internet and Kyoto University—reflects the collaboration between industry and academia that characterizes much of the materials informatics field.

Why This Matters: The Synthesis Bottleneck

Materials discovery has advanced rapidly on the computational side—property prediction from composition and structure is now routine for many material classes. But synthesis planning remains largely manual, dependent on expert knowledge buried in literature.

The Unstructured Knowledge Problem

Consider a typical synthesis paper: a paragraph might describe heating precursors to a specific temperature, holding for a duration, cooling at a controlled rate, then performing a characterization step. The procedure spans multiple sentences, uses domain-specific terminology, and embeds critical parameters within narrative text.

For an AI system to learn from this, it needs to:

  1. Identify that this is a synthesis procedure (not background or results)
  2. Extract each discrete operation
  3. Understand which materials are inputs and outputs for each step
  4. Capture parameter values (temperatures, times, concentrations)
  5. Represent the sequence and dependencies correctly

MatPROV tackles this by leveraging LLMs’ natural language understanding capabilities, combined with the formal structure of PROV-DM, to create a standardized representation.

From Text to Graph: The MatPROV Pipeline

Scientific Paper Text
         |
         v
LLM Parsing (identify procedures, extract entities)
         |
         v
PROV-DM Mapping (assign roles: entity, activity, agent)
         |
         v
Directed Graph (nodes and edges)

This graph representation enables several applications:

  • Computational analysis: Compare procedures across papers, identify common patterns
  • Similarity search: Find synthesis methods that use similar approaches
  • Integration with ELNs: Electronic laboratory notebooks can automatically capture provenance
  • Automation potential: Structured graphs can be converted to executable scripts for robotic labs

NeurIPS and AI4Mat: A Prestigious Venue

The acceptance of this work to the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2025 signals that the research meets technical standards for contribution in the machine learning community.

NeurIPS (Neural Information Processing Systems), established in 1987, is the premier machine learning conference. Acceptance to the main conference or its workshops requires peer review and technical rigor. The AI4Mat Workshop, started in 2022, specifically focuses on applying machine learning to materials science problems.

This venue matters because it brings materials informatics to the mainstream ML community. The workshop audience includes both materials scientists seeking ML tools and ML researchers looking for applications—exactly the interdisciplinary audience for provenance-aware materials data.

The workshop format allows for focused discussion on challenges specific to materials ML: small datasets, complex physics, and the need for interpretable models that scientists can trust.

Looking Ahead: From Papers to Pipelines

What are the potential impacts if the MatPROV approach scales across the materials literature?

Potential Applications

  1. Large-scale synthesis analysis: With thousands of procedures extracted as structured graphs, researchers could analyze patterns across material classes, identifying which synthesis routes are most common or which parameters correlate with successful outcomes.

  2. Robotic laboratory integration: Structured procedure graphs can be converted to executable automation scripts. A robot could read a synthesis graph, map operations to available equipment, and execute the procedure automatically.

  3. Improved electronic laboratory notebooks: ELNs that automatically capture provenance would make experiments more reproducible. Instead of free-form notes, the notebook would maintain a formal graph of what was done, with what, by whom, and when.

  4. ML models on structured data: Models trained on structured procedure representations could learn to predict synthesis conditions for new materials, rather than just predicting properties from composition.

Challenges to Address

The research faces several challenges:

  • Extraction accuracy: LLMs can miss domain-specific nuances or misinterpret procedural language
  • Terminology diversity: Different communities use different terms for similar operations
  • Scaling to diverse materials: Ceramics, polymers, and metals each have specialized synthesis techniques
  • Validation: How to verify that extracted graphs accurately represent the intended procedure

A Quiet Month, A Steady Advance

November was notably quiet for major materials discovery announcements. This single accepted paper highlights an important truth: fundamental research infrastructure—datasets, standards, extraction methods—often advances steadily between headline-grabbing discoveries. The work that enables the next generation of AI-driven materials labs happens incrementally, paper by paper, workshop by workshop.

MatPROV is one step toward making materials synthesis knowledge computable. Whether this particular approach scales remains to be seen, but the direction—using LLMs to extract structured, standards-compliant representations from literature—will likely influence how materials informatics bridges the gap between published knowledge and automated discovery.
