item.content:encoded:
This month brought a coordinated surge in quantum hardware announcements. IBM unveiled two new processors targeting fault tolerance by 2029. Quantinuum launched Helios, which it calls the most accurate quantum computer. IQM introduced the Halocene line for error correction research. Behind these product releases, researchers achieved breakthroughs in qubit coherence, quantum networking, and error correction that could fundamentally change the scaling trajectory.

This comprehensive review covers 88 articles published in November 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing.

The Hardware Wave

The most visible story this month was a coordinated wave of quantum processor announcements from leading hardware companies, all converging on error correction as the priority.

IBM unveiled two new quantum processors in November. Nighthawk features 120 qubits with 218 tunable couplers —20% more than the previous Heron processor—enabling 30% more complex calculations . The chip supports up to 5,000 two-qubit gates , with iterations planned to reach 7,500 gates by end of 2026 and 15,000 gates by 2028 .

The second processor, Loon, incorporates hardware designed specifically for fault tolerance , including low-loss routing layers and qubit reset capabilities . IBM’s error decoding achieves 480-nanosecond latency . The company targets quantum advantage by 2026 and fully fault-tolerant quantum computing by 2029 , with a planned 2,000-qubit Starling processor for that year. Both processors use 300mm wafer fabrication , which halves manufacturing time and enables a 10-times increase in physical complexity .

Quantinuum launched Helios, a system the company calls “easily the most powerful quantum computer on Earth” . The system features 98 physical qubits achieving 48 fully error-corrected logical qubits at a 2:1 physical-to-logical ratio —significantly better than the 10:1 ratio commonly assumed. The system achieved 99.921% two-qubit gate fidelity across all qubit pairs and 99.9975% single-qubit gate fidelity . Helios uses redesigned junction ion-trap hardware with barium ions and a new software stack featuring the Guppy programming language . Enterprise partners including SoftBank , JPMorgan Chase , and Google used the system during early access for finance and materials science applications. The system was used to simulate a superconducting metal , revealing new electron behavior.

IQM Quantum Computers launched the Halocene product line, designed specifically for quantum error correction research . The first release is a 150-qubit system with advanced error correction features, scheduled for commercial availability by end of 2026 . The system supports research on up to five logical qubits and incorporates the company’s IQM Crystal QPU with 99.7% physical two-qubit gate fidelity . Future product releases target qubit counts beyond 1,000 .

China’s Hanyuan-1 quantum computer achieved commercialization in November, with orders worth over 40 million yuan ($5.6 million) including an export order to Pakistan . The system features 100 qubits with 99.9% single-qubit gate fidelity and 98% two-qubit gate fidelity . Notably, it operates without cryogenic refrigeration , reducing maintenance and energy consumption by over 90% compared to superconducting systems . The entire machine fits into three standard racks . The system has been integrated with the Atomic Quantum Computing Cloud Platform , connecting 50 universities and enterprises . The team aims to provide large-scale computing services by 2027 .

Other November hardware announcements included IonQ announcing a record-low error rate above 99.99% for two-qubit gates and a method to skip cooling steps to improve speed , and Oxford Ionics introducing a multicore approach using trapped ions . D-Wave made its Advantage2 system available to U.S. government customers , adding another option for federal agencies exploring quantum applications.

Under the Hood: Error Correction Advances

While hardware announcements grabbed headlines, the underlying research advances may prove more significant for the field’s trajectory. November brought breakthroughs in qubit coherence, magic state distillation, and fault-tolerant architectures.

Coherence Breakthrough

Princeton University engineers published work on a new superconducting qubit achieving over 1 millisecond of coherence time —three times longer than the previous lab record and nearly 15 times longer than the industry standard . The design uses tantalum on a silicon substrate and is compatible with existing processors like Google’s . The researchers project the design could improve system reliability by up to 1,000 times for Google’s Willow processor and by 1 billion times for a hypothetical 1,000-qubit computer .

The advance addresses the core bottleneck in error correction: longer coherence means fewer errors occur during computation, reducing the overhead for correction. The work represents the largest single advance in qubit coherence time in over a decade . The paper was published in Nature .

System Coherence Time Improvement Significance
Princeton tantalum transmon 1 ms 3x best lab, 15x industry Reduces error correction overhead
Previous lab record ~0.33 ms Baseline Published research result
Industry standard ~0.07 ms Baseline Current commercial systems

Optimizing Distillation

Researchers from MIT’s Center for Theoretical Physics achieved theoretically optimal scaling for magic state distillation , reaching a scaling exponent of zero —meaning constant overhead. This resolves a long-standing theoretical problem by proving that the number of noisy input states needed per high-quality output state does not have to grow as error rates decrease. The previous best scaling, achieved in 2017, was approximately 0.678 .

The work, published in Nature Physics , bridges a gap between theoretical qudit systems and practical qubit-based quantum computers. Magic state distillation is essential for implementing non-Clifford gates (such as T gates), which are required for universal quantum computation but cannot be performed directly with error-corrected Clifford operations. Constant overhead means significantly fewer physical resources are needed for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Fault-Tolerant Architectures

Researchers published experimental work on a fault-tolerant neutral-atom architecture using reconfigurable arrays of up to 448 neutral atoms . They demonstrated below-threshold error correction with surface codes, showing 2.14x lower error per round for a distance-5 code compared to distance-3. The work demonstrated logical entanglement via transversal gates and achieved a two-orders-of-magnitude increase in cycle rates through mid-circuit qubit reuse. The team achieved 0.46% bit-flip error rate and 0.24% loss rate in non-destructive readout. With loss information and machine learning decoding, they achieved 1.73x better QEC performance compared to conventional methods.

Separate work proposed a fiber array architecture for atom quantum computing that enables fully independent control of individual atoms . Researchers experimentally demonstrated trapping and independent control of ten single atoms , achieving 99.66% average fidelity for individually addressed single-qubit gates and 99.61% for simultaneous arbitrary single-qubit gates on four qubits . This approach enables high-rate, highly parallel gate operations, which could accelerate quantum algorithm execution on neutral atom systems.

Connecting the Quantum Internet

University of Chicago researchers extended the maximum distance for quantum computer connections to 2,000 kilometers —a 200X improvement over the previous record of approximately 10 km. The breakthrough uses molecular-beam epitaxy to create high-purity rare-earth doped crystals , which enhance coherence from 0.1 milliseconds to over 10 milliseconds . In one instance, the team demonstrated 24 milliseconds of coherence , which would enable 4,000 km theoretical connection distance . The research was published in Nature Communications .

Separately, University of Chicago scientists built a molecular qubit using erbium that transmits quantum information at telecom wavelengths , making it compatible with existing fiber-optic networks . The qubit acts as a bridge between magnetism and optics, storing information magnetically and being read out optically. The molecular qubit is 100,000 times smaller than a human hair , enabling integration with silicon chips. This research was published in Science .

Google Quantum AI published a five-stage roadmap to guide quantum computing research from abstract theory to practical applications. The framework highlights a critical bottleneck in demonstrating quantum advantage for real-world problems (Stage III) and calls for cultural and funding shifts to support cross-disciplinary work. The team proposes using AI tools to help map known quantum algorithmic advantages to concrete application areas.

Quantum at Work: Early Applications

Simulation Milestones

A team from the Jülich Supercomputing Center and NVIDIA achieved the first full simulation of a 50-qubit universal quantum computer —surpassing the previous record of 48 qubits set in 2022 . The simulation ran on Europe’s first exascale supercomputer, JUPITER , using more than 16,000 NVIDIA GH200 Superchips and requiring approximately 2 petabytes of memory . This enables high-fidelity testing of quantum algorithms such as VQE and QAOA for chemistry, materials science, and optimization applications.

U.S. Department of Energy researchers performed one of the largest digital quantum simulations on IBM quantum hardware, using scalable quantum circuits to simulate a one-dimensional quantum electrodynamics model with over 100 qubits . They achieved percent-level accuracy in simulating vacuum properties and preparing hadron pulses, enabling simulations of matter under extreme conditions beyond classical computation.

A U.S.-Canadian research team used a trapped ion quantum computer to simulate a simplified one-dimensional phase diagram of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) . This work could provide a foundation for understanding extreme environments like the inside of neutron stars or the early universe, which are intractable for classical computers. The team introduced a new type of ancillae register to make quantum computations more efficient.

Photonic Advances

Researchers at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) experimentally realized universal quantum gates and generated a six-qubit entangled state using a photonic quantum walk system. They achieved this by encoding three qubits onto a single photon via polarization and path encoding, then entangling two such photons. This deterministic approach using linear optics advances the potential for scalable, room-temperature photonic quantum computing.

KAIST researchers developed an efficient Multimode Quantum Process Tomography technique for optical quantum computers, reducing the data needed to characterize complex quantum operations. They achieved the first experimental characterization of a 16-mode optical quantum process , overcoming previous limitations.

Practical Tests

D-Wave demonstrated significant advantages over classical supercomputers , claiming to solve complex simulations in minutes instead of nearly a million years with minimal energy consumption. The company reported electricity costs of less than $1 for simulations that would require as much electricity as the world uses in a year on a classical supercomputer. These capabilities are being applied through partnerships with organizations like JSC and Japan Tobacco .

Haiqu, a quantum software company, demonstrated that quantum computers can detect anomalies more efficiently than classical systems using an IBM Quantum Heron processor. Their proprietary quantum encoding technique loaded over 500 features into quantum circuits on 128 qubits , showing potential for quantum advantage in machine learning for finance and healthcare applications.

Speculative Ideas

Researchers from King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) proposed using blimps to lift quantum data centers to the stratosphere , where the natural cold reduces the energy needed to cool qubits. The floating platforms, called QC-HAPs , would be powered by solar energy and communicate via light beams. At 20 km altitude where temperatures reach -50 degrees C , the concept could achieve 21% energy cost savings for ion trap quantum computers. This remains a proposal rather than an active development program.

The Partnership Network

North America

IBM and Cisco announced a collaboration to develop networked distributed quantum computing , targeting an initial proof-of-concept by 2030 . The partnership aims to link large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers with a long-term vision of enabling a quantum computing internet by the late 2030s . They plan demonstrations of multiple connected QPUs within the next three years .

California Governor Gavin Newsom announced Quantum California, a statewide initiative backed by $4 million in funding to strengthen California’s leadership in quantum technology. The initiative aligns UC Berkeley, UC San Diego, UCLA, Stanford, and Caltech with industry leaders including Google, Microsoft, and Amazon .

PsiQuantum selected Jacobs as the Owner’s Representative for a new quantum computing facility in Chicago . The project involves building an intermediate-scale test system and progressing toward a utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer. Construction has begun on the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park (IQMP) , a 128-acre campus with the first phase occupying 30 acres and scheduled for completion in 2027 .

PsiQuantum and Lockheed Martin expanded their partnership to apply quantum computing to complex optimization problems, including the “cocktail party problem” of separating overlapping signals in defense applications.

IonQ announced a partnership with the University of Chicago to advance quantum workforce development and research, including access to IonQ systems for academic research.

Microsoft announced expansion of its quantum operations in Denmark , investing in facilities and talent to advance topological qubit development. The company also opened a new quantum lab in Chicago , expanding its physical research presence.

Europe

The European Space Agency (ESA) selected Equal1 to install a Hybrid Quantum Computing System for Earth Observation , deploying Equal1’s Bell-1 Quantum Computer to accelerate processing of complex Earth Observation data. The 6-qubit system consumes 1,600 W and is designed for seamless integration with ESA’s existing HPC infrastructure.

SDT Inc. joined the QuEra Quantum Alliance to advance the commercialization and industrial adoption of neutral-atom quantum computing . SDT, as South Korea’s only full-stack quantum company, will contribute its Quantum Design & Manufacturing (QDM) framework to accelerate practical deployment. QuEra recently installed a $41 million neutral-atom quantum computer at Japan’s AIST.

SemiQon and Conductor Technology announced a partnership to accelerate the manufacture of silicon-based quantum processors using semiconductor industry techniques.

Alice & Bob and Thales expanded their collaboration to develop error-corrected quantum solutions for aerospace and defense applications.

Asia-Pacific & Middle East

NTT and OptQC signed a collaboration agreement to develop scalable optical quantum computers with a goal of achieving one million qubits by 2030 . The partnership combines NTT’s optical communication technologies with OptQC’s expertise in building room-temperature quantum systems. OptQC is currently developing a 10,000-qubit system with its first commercial optical quantum computer scheduled for completion in April 2026 . NTT’s optical amplification technology achieves quantum entanglement generation rates 1,000 times faster than conventional methods.

Saudi Arabia is establishing its first quantum computing capabilities through a partnership between Saudi Aramco and Pasqal. The initiative will deploy Pasqal’s neutral-atom quantum computers for energy industry applications, making Saudi Arabia the first country in the Middle East with commercial quantum computing access.

Qilimanjaro announced expansion into the Asia-Pacific market with a new headquarters in Singapore.

Market Dynamics

The industry’s underlying economics shifted in November, with one major IPO and a sobering assessment of manufacturing challenges.

Xanadu Quantum Technologies announced it will go public via a business combination with Crane Harbor Acquisition Corp. , valuing the company at $3.6 billion . This makes it the first publicly traded pure-play photonic quantum computing company . The transaction includes $500 million in gross proceeds from the business combination and $275 million from a PIPE offering . Xanadu’s achievements include quantum supremacy with its 216-qubit Borealis system , which completed a task in 2 minutes that would take a classical supercomputer 7 million years . The company’s PennyLane software holds 47% usage share among quantum programmers.

Rigetti Computing reported Q3 2025 financial results showing sequential revenue growth of 5.6% but a year-over-year decline of 20.6% . The company unveiled an aggressive roadmap targeting 1,000+ qubits by 2027 . Rigetti reported strong liquidity with $558.9 million in cash and investments as of quarter-end, increasing to approximately $600 million by November 6, 2025 .

John Martinis, the Google quantum computing pioneer, published a critique arguing that quantum computing progress is stalled due to manufacturing limitations . He emphasized the need to shift from hand-built lab devices to integrated, factory-produced chips to reach the million-qubit scale needed for general-purpose machines. Martinis noted that Google’s quantum chips grew from 53 qubits to 105 qubits over six years —doubling rather than exponential growth. He called for abandoning outdated techniques like the “lift-off” process and developing cryogenic integrated circuits . Without this manufacturing overhaul, he warned, the field risks remaining “trapped in a jungle of wires” and decades away from practical systems .

Microsoft announced major investments in quantum facilities , including expansion in Denmark for topological qubit development and a new quantum lab in Chicago.

J.P. Morgan reported that global quantum venture investment increased 17x over the past decade , with significant acceleration in 2025. The bank identified error correction and fault tolerance as key thresholds for practical applications.

Beyond Hardware

Software & Access

Kvantify launched Qrunch, a quantum computing platform designed for chemical and biological engineering . The platform abstracts quantum complexity into an intuitive interface, allowing scientists to build quantum algorithms without quantum expertise. Qrunch has demonstrated up to 80 qubit simulations with 3-4x improvement in problem-size capacity . The platform integrates with gate-based quantum computers including superconducting systems via Amazon Braket and IQM systems .

QSolid made its prototype quantum computer available for first external testing , providing researchers with access to superconducting quantum hardware for experimental validation.

Policy & Security

Quantum computing was actively showcased at COP30 with the release of a sustainability report by the Sustainability Quantum Working Group, which includes 60+ experts . The report demonstrates how quantum systems are addressing concrete problems in energy, materials, and climate modeling.

The UK government’s Critical Minerals Strategy 2035 aims to secure critical minerals for high-tech industries by boosting domestic production, midstream processing, and recycling. The strategy targets 20% of UK mineral demand to be met via recycled materials by 2035 and includes a 50 million pound funding program . Quantum technologies, which depend on materials like rare earths and ultra-pure metals, will benefit from reduced supply-chain vulnerabilities.

Computer scientists are developing post-quantum cryptography using mathematical problems such as structured lattices and hash functions to secure data against future quantum attacks. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) is considering four problems for post-quantum cryptography standards. Experts emphasize the importance of cryptographic agility to protect against future quantum threats.

Industry Reflections

Nature Materials interviewed Pascale Senellart-Mardon, co-founder of Quandela, about photonic quantum computing technologies and the challenges of juggling academia and industry.

Several publications published retrospectives on 2025 quantum breakthroughs , noting the shift from pure research to early deployment with commercial systems like Quantinuum’s Helios and demonstrations of quantum advantage. The year saw quantum computing equity funding reach $3.77 billion in the first nine months of 2025, compared to $1.3 billion in all of 2024 . National government investment reached $10 billion by April 2025 , compared to $1.8 billion in all of 2024 .

Network World reported that enterprise adoption is accelerating, with 60% of business leaders actively investing in or exploring quantum AI . A D-Wave survey found that 81% of leaders said they’ve reached the limit with classical computers , and 53% are planning to build quantum computing into workflows . Quantum computing could potentially unlock $250 billion in market value across pharma, finance, logistics, and materials science.

Error Correction Focus: 2025-2029 Roadmaps

Company 2025 System Target Path
IBM Nighthawk (120q) + Loon (112q) Fault tolerance by 2029 Square grid, error-corrected logical qubits
Quantinuum Helios (98q / 48 logical) Generative Quantum AI Ion-trap, 2:1 physical:logical ratio
IQM Halocene (150q) Error correction research Superconducting architecture
NTT-OPTQC Optical system 1M qubits by 2030 Photonic, telecom wavelength

The Road to 2029

November’s developments reveal quantum computing at a transition point. The hardware announcements represent real systems with specified availability dates, not theoretical roadmaps. IBM’s Nighthawk and Loon processors are available now. Quantinuum’s Helios is commercially deployed. IQM’s Halocene has a 2026 commercial availability target. These are engineering milestones, not physics experiments.

The error correction advances are equally substantive. Princeton’s 1ms qubit directly addresses the coherence bottleneck that determines how many operations can be performed before errors accumulate. The optimal magic state distillation scaling resolves a theoretical problem that has constrained fault-tolerant architectures for two decades. The neutral-atom fault-tolerant architecture demonstrates below-threshold error correction with surface codes—the gold standard for quantum error correction.

But John Martinis’s manufacturing critique is the necessary reality check. His observation that Google’s chips grew from 53 to 105 qubits over six years—roughly doubling, not exponential—contradicts narratives of rapid scaling. His argument that the field needs to transition from hand-built lab devices to factory-produced chips resonates because IBM’s 300mm wafer fabrication announcement represents exactly that type of manufacturing advance.

The quantum networking breakthrough extends the potential scale of quantum systems beyond single machines. University of Chicago’s 2,000 km connection distance and the erbium molecular qubit’s compatibility with existing fiber networks mean quantum computers could eventually be networked globally. IBM and Cisco’s collaboration to build networked distributed quantum computing by 2030 is a direct response to this possibility.

The field is transitioning from physics experiments to engineering challenges. The 2029 fault-tolerance target that IBM, Quantinuum, and others are coalescing around is aggressive but—for the first time—backed by coherent technical plans rather than speculative roadmaps. The question is whether manufacturing can scale fast enough to realize those plans.

The next three years will determine whether 2029 marks the beginning of the fault-tolerant era or another milestone on a longer timeline. What November made clear is that the path forward requires advances on three fronts simultaneously: better qubits (Princeton’s 1ms coherence), better error correction (optimal magic state distillation, below-threshold surface codes), and better manufacturing (IBM’s 300mm wafers, Martinis’s cryogenic integrated circuits). All three showed progress this month.

item.title: AI's October Evolution: From Laboratory Assistant to Autonomous Scientist
item.description:
A $300 million seed round for Periodic Labs underscores a fundamental shift: AI is no longer just assisting materials discovery—it’s running entire labs autonomously. A comprehensive review this month shows AI now drives every stage of research, from hypothesis to synthesis. But as the field generates millions of new materials, a critical question emerges: how do we validate what AI creates?

This review covers 18 articles published between October 1-30, 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI-driven materials discovery.
item.content:encoded:
A $300 million seed round for Periodic Labs underscores a fundamental shift: AI is no longer just assisting materials discovery—it’s running entire labs autonomously. A comprehensive review this month shows AI now drives every stage of research, from hypothesis to synthesis. But as the field generates millions of new materials, a critical question emerges: how do we validate what AI creates?

This review covers 18 articles published between October 1-30, 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI-driven materials discovery.

The Big Story: $300M Bet on Autonomous Material Discovery

Periodic Labs emerged from stealth on October 21 with a $300 million seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz, marking one of the most ambitious and well-funded efforts yet to merge AI with real-world scientific experimentation . The company was founded by Liam Fedus, an influential researcher at OpenAI, and Ekin Dogus Cubuk, a leading scientist at Google Brain. They have assembled a team of elite researchers from top AI and science labs, including angel investors Jeff Bezos, Elad Gil, Eric Schmidt, and Jeff Dean. Other investors include Felicis, DST, NVentures (Nvidia’s venture arm), Accel, General Catalyst, and Microsoft.

The company aims to fuse large language models, robotics, and physics simulations to create an automated system for material discovery, starting with next-generation superconductors as its first target . The funding size signals major investor confidence in autonomous material discovery as a commercial frontier.

This isn’t just one company’s bet—it reflects a broader transformation. A comprehensive review published in ACS Nano on October 27 finds that AI, machine learning, and deep learning now autonomously drive all stages of materials research, from discovery to optimization. Researchers from KAIST, Drexel University, Northwestern University, the University of St Andrews, and the University of Tennessee collaborated on the review, which proposes an AI-based catalyst search platform and the concept of a self-driving lab where robots conduct experiments.

Led by Professor Seungbum Hong of KAIST and lead author Benediktus Madika, the review positions AI as “the new language of materials science,” offering a roadmap for accelerating innovation in core industries like batteries and semiconductors. The review marks a paradigm shift where AI “transcends being a mere tool to become an autonomous ’thinking researcher’ that can dramatically accelerate materials innovation.”

The Scale Challenge: 2.2M Materials and Counting

The excitement around autonomous material discovery must be balanced against a hard reality: Google DeepMind used deep learning to discover 2.2 million new crystalline materials, but as Nature asked on October 1 , are they any good?

The GNoME (Graph Networks for Materials Exploration) AI system discovered these novel crystal structures, but validation remains the bottleneck. Only 700 of the 2.2 million predicted crystals have been synthesized in labs to date, according to Interesting Engineering . Of the full set, 380,000 are predicted to be stable crystal structure candidates—still an overwhelming number for experimental verification.

The Innovation News Network reports that additional AI systems are generating even more candidates. SCIGEN (Structural Constraint Integration in a GENerative model) has generated 10 million candidate materials, of which 1 million passed stability screenings. A new dataset called OMol25 contains 100 million DFT evaluations across 83 million unique molecular systems.

This creates a central tension: AI can generate candidates at unprecedented scale, but experimental verification can’t keep pace. Autonomous labs are making progress—one system produced 41 new compounds in 17 days, and another conducted 3,025 predicted experiments in 24 hours. But the average timeline for translating a new material from concept to commercial product remains 10-20 years.

As the field grapples with this bottleneck, a crucial insight is emerging: human judgment remains crucial for evaluating feasibility and guiding innovation, ensuring that AI-driven advances translate into viable technologies.

Research Highlights: What AI Discovered This Month

Thermal Management Breakthroughs

The most striking thermal materials discovery came from the University of Houston, where researchers discovered that high-quality boron arsenide crystals achieve thermal conductivity exceeding 2,100 W/mK—potentially surpassing diamond, according to research published in Materials Today on October 10 . This overturns existing theories: revised models had previously capped boron arsenide’s thermal conductivity at 1,360 W/mK, and samples with defects measured only 1,300 W/mK.

The discovery involves collaboration with UC Santa Barbara and Boston College, with Qorvo and a $2.8 million National Science Foundation grant supporting the work. Led by Professor Zhifeng Ren at UH and physicist David Broido at Boston College, with Bolin Liao leading the NSF grant at UCSB, the breakthrough could lead to advanced semiconductors with superior thermal management for electronics like cell phones and data centers.

Separately, a team from Wuhan University developed an interpretable deep learning framework that accelerates the discovery of materials with tailored thermal properties. Their approach accurately predicts lattice thermal conductivity and identified four high-performance thermal management materials (three thermal conductors and one thermal insulator). The framework bridges computational efficiency and physical understanding by integrating density functional theory (DFT), the Boltzmann transport equation (BTE), molecular dynamics simulations, graph neural networks, and unsupervised k-means clustering.

Published online in Materials Futures, the work by researchers Yuxuan Zeng, Wei Cao, Yijing Zuo, Tan Peng, Yue Hou, Ling Miao, Ziyu Wang, and Jing Shi speeds up the development of efficient thermoelectric devices and thermal control systems.

Superconductors and Magnetic Materials

Penn State scientists have developed a new theory-driven method to predict superconductors, potentially paving the way to materials that conduct electricity perfectly at higher temperatures. Professor Zi-Kui Liu and his team combine density functional theory with zentropy theory to bridge the gap between conventional Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory and the search for high-temperature superconductors.

Published in Superconductor Science and Technology on July 18, 2025, the team successfully predicted superconductivity in conventional materials and even in metals like copper, silver, and gold at ultra-low temperatures. They have been building a comprehensive database of 5 million materials to support this work, funded by the Department of Energy’s Basic Energy Science division under the Theory of Condensed Matter program.

In magnetic materials, researchers published the Northeast Materials Database (NEMAD) in Nature on October 24 , using Large Language Models to extract and compile data from scientific articles. The database contains 67,573 magnetic materials entries, created through automated data extraction using ChemDataExtractor, the Snowball algorithm, BERT, GPT-4o, and Google Gemini OCR.

The team trained machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Ensemble Neural Network) on this database, achieving 90% accuracy in classifying ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and non-magnetic materials. For predicting transition temperatures, they achieved an R² of 0.87 with a 56K mean absolute error for Curie temperature, and an R² of 0.83 with a 38K mean absolute error for Néel temperature. The models identified 25 ferromagnetic candidates with predicted Curie temperature above 500K and 13 antiferromagnetic candidates with predicted Néel temperature above 100K.

Energy Storage

Researchers at the New Jersey Institute of Technology used generative AI to discover five new porous materials for multivalent-ion batteries, which could offer a cost-effective and high-energy alternative to lithium-ion batteries. Led by Professor Dibakar Datta, the team used a crystal diffusion variational autoencoder (CDVAE) combined with a large language model and quantum mechanical simulations to discover the new porous transition metal oxide structures.

From Automation to Collaboration

The most significant shift in self-driving labs isn’t just automation—it’s collaboration. Boston University researcher Keith Brown is transforming self-driving labs from isolated, automated systems into open, community-driven platforms .

Brown’s MAMA BEAR (Bayesian experimental autonomous researcher) system has conducted 25,000 experiments since 2023, discovering a material with 75.2% energy absorption efficiency. Through collaboration with Cornell University led by Professor Peter Frazier, the team improved mechanical energy absorption benchmarks from 26 J/g to 55 J/g.

The dataset from these experiments has been downloaded 89 times from BU Libraries as of June 2025, demonstrating demand for shared experimental data. Brown is now expanding this work through a multi-university NSF Artificial Intelligence Materials Institute (AI-MI) that includes CUNY and Princeton University.

At BU, other professors involved include Wenchao Li, Emily Whiting, Sean Andersson, and Emma Lejeune, with Yannis Paschalidis directing the Hariri Institute. The initiative combines AI, robotics, and human collaboration to democratize experimental science through FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data practices and the emerging AI Materials Science Ecosystem (AIMS-EC).

This collaborative model extends to industry. SES AI Corporation announced Molecular Universe 1.0 (MU-1) , an AI-powered platform that accelerates battery material discovery from years to tens of minutes. The platform offers a one-million-molecule database for public tier users and a 200-million-molecule database for enterprise subscribers.

Founded by CEO Qichao Hu, SES AI’s platform uses GPT-5 models and molecular dynamics simulations with polarizable force fields. A live demo launched October 20, 2025, showcasing end-to-end capabilities including literature research (Ask), molecule search (Map and Search), formulation search (Formulate), and cell performance prediction (Predict), as detailed by Battery Technology .

The vision of AI-run labs extends further. At the Singapore Week of Innovation and Technology 2025, Radical AI CEO Joseph Krause discussed how AI-driven laboratories could accelerate materials discovery up to 370 times faster than human researchers , paving the way for breakthroughs in clean energy, aerospace, and nuclear fusion.

Company/Platform Focus Notable This Month
Periodic Labs Autonomous material discovery $300M seed round for LLMs + robotics + physics
SES AI Battery material discovery MU-1 platform with 200M molecule database
Google DeepMind Materials generation 2.2M crystalline materials discovered
BU MAMA BEAR Self-driving lab 25,000 experiments conducted

Emerging Approaches

CrystalFlow, published in Nature on October 20 , introduces a flow-based generative model for crystalline materials combining Continuous Normalizing Flows and Conditional Flow Matching with graph-based equivariant neural networks and symmetry-aware data representations. The model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art diffusion models like Crystal Diffusion VAE, DiffCSP, MatterGen, and UniMat, but is approximately an order of magnitude more efficient. It also supports conditional generation for specific pressures or material properties.

The exa-AMD framework, developed by Los Alamos National Laboratory, Ames National Laboratory, and Iowa State University , accelerates materials discovery by integrating artificial intelligence and high-performance computing. Led by scientists Weiyi Xia, Maxim Moraru, and Ying Wai Li at Los Alamos and Cai-Zhuang Wang at Ames, the framework automates the entire process from elemental input to predicting stable material structures and updating phase diagrams. It uses machine learning, density functional theory, genetic algorithms, and the Parsl library for high-throughput screening on exascale computers.

Google achieved the first-ever verifiable quantum advantage using its Willow quantum processor and a new algorithm called Quantum Echoes. CEO Sundar Pichai announced that the algorithm ran 13,000 times faster than the best classical algorithm on a supercomputer and can model atomic interactions in molecules, paving the way for applications in drug discovery and materials science. The breakthrough’s verifiability sets it apart, allowing other quantum computers to reproduce the results.

Professor Fumiyasu Oba at the Institute of Science Tokyo uses computational science and data science to discover new materials for energy conservation and carbon neutrality, such as the nitride semiconductor CaZn2N2. His work integrates first-principles calculations with materials informatics and machine learning, having screened 1,000 hypothetical candidate materials to discover CaZn2N2 in 2016. In 2024, his team developed a machine learning predictive model using 3,000 surfaces of inorganic materials. Oba has received multiple awards for this work, including the 2025 Commendation for Science and Technology by Japan’s Minister of Education.

The Department of Materials Science and Engineering at Uppsala universitet hosted a seminar in late September 2025 to explore AI applications in materials science. Researchers demonstrated AI’s use in automating bubble detection in microphysiological systems and accelerating the discovery of new solar materials through the Self-Driving Lab BERTHA. Led by Professors Cecilia Persson, Jens Sjölund, Eric Berg, and researchers Nadia Koriakina and Jonathan Scragg, the event aimed to inspire more researchers to integrate AI into their projects.

Looking Ahead: The Validation Frontier

October showed both the promise and the challenge of AI-driven materials discovery. The field has achieved unprecedented scale—2.2 million materials from GNoME, 10 million from SCIGEN—massive investment—$300 million for Periodic Labs—and autonomous systems that conduct experiments 370 times faster than humans.

But the central question is validation. As Nature asked, are these materials any good? Only 700 of 2.2 million candidates have been synthesized. The field’s next frontier isn’t generating more candidates—it’s building the experimental and computational infrastructure to verify which ones are actually useful.

The shift from isolated automation to collaborative platforms suggests the community recognizes this. Boston University’s MAMA BEAR sharing its dataset, SES AI opening its molecular database, and the multi-university NSF AI-MI institute all point toward a more open approach. Success will require combining AI’s generative capacity with scalable validation methods—whether through high-throughput robotics, quantum computing like Google’s Willow processor, or new computational frameworks like exa-AMD and CrystalFlow.

The vision of AI as an “autonomous thinking researcher” is compelling. But for now, human judgment remains essential for evaluating feasibility and guiding innovation. The most promising path forward combines AI’s scale with human insight—and increasingly, with shared platforms that let the entire field contribute to validation.

This comprehensive review covers 87 articles published between October 1-31, 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing. This month, Caltech built a 6,100-qubit array at room temperature, Google unveiled verifiable quantum advantage with its Willow chip, and NVIDIA announced NVQLink to tightly couple GPUs with quantum processors. The field is making measurable progress on multiple fronts.

The Numbers: Scale and Speed

The most striking quantitative milestone of the month came from Caltech, where researchers led by professor Manuel Endres built a neutral-atom quantum array with 6,100 qubits - nearly 10 times larger than the previous record of 1,180 qubits. The system operates at room temperature and achieved a 12.6-second coherence time while maintaining 99.98% accuracy in manipulating individual atoms. The array uses approximately 12,000 laser tweezers arranged in a two-zone “zone-based quantum computing” architecture, with 6,139 atoms stably loaded into the grid.

The significance lies in the combination of scale and stability. Previous neutral-atom systems faced trade-offs between qubit count and coherence time. The Caltech team demonstrated that both can scale together: they maintained record coherence times for hyperfine qubits in an optical tweezer array while achieving qubit counts an order of magnitude beyond prior systems. The researchers estimate scaling to over 10,000 qubits in the near future, with a potential path to one million qubits within a decade.

Google’s Willow quantum chip, featuring a 105-qubit superconducting array, achieved what the company calls the first verifiable quantum advantage. Running the “Quantum Echoes” algorithm (measuring out-of-time-order correlators), Willow completed a calculation in 2 hours that would take an estimated 150 years on the Frontier supercomputer - a 13,000x speedup. The chip achieved 99.97% single-qubit gate fidelity, 99.88% entangling gate fidelity, and 99.5% readout fidelity, with gate operations running in tens to hundreds of nanoseconds.

However, researchers expressed skepticism about the broader implications. The calculation, while verifiable, remains highly specialized. The verification method itself requires another quantum computer, which limits immediate practical utility. Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin noted that this represents progress on a specific class of problems rather than general quantum advantage. The Nature news article covering the announcement highlighted ongoing debates about what constitutes meaningful quantum advantage and whether such demonstrations accelerate the path to practical applications.

System Type Qubits Significance
Caltech Neutral-Atom Array Research 6,100 Room-temperature operation, 12.6-second coherence
Google Willow Superconducting 105 First verifiable quantum advantage claim
IBM System Two (Spain) Superconducting 156 First System Two in Europe
China Zuchongzhi 3.0 Superconducting 105 Commercial cloud deployment
Quandela Lucy Photonic 12 Universal digital photonic system

The Real Bottleneck: Error Correction

Quantum computers are inherently error-prone; fixing these errors is the main obstacle to practical use. Multiple advances this month addressed this bottleneck from different angles.

Algorithmic Advances

Researchers published a new technique called Algorithmic Fault Tolerance (AFT) that can reduce error correction overhead by 10-100 times. The method, tested in simulations by QuEra , restructures algorithms to detect errors on the fly rather than pausing for separate correction cycles. Yuval Boger, QuEra’s chief commercial officer, said this “moves the timeline forward significantly” for practical quantum computers. The research results were published in Nature on September 24, with hardware tests expected in 2026-2027.

Hardware Improvements

IonQ announced a world-record two-qubit gate fidelity of 99.99%, achieved without resource-intensive ground-state cooling. This breakthrough addresses a major speed bottleneck in trapped-ion quantum computing. In previous QCCD (Quantum Charge Coupled Device) demonstrations, runtime was dominated by ion movement (~27%) and cooling (~68%), with only ~2% spent on actual quantum gate operations. The new approach allows faster ion cooling and movement, potentially enabling order-of-magnitude faster computations. IonQ’s roadmap targets scaling to millions of qubits by 2030.

Researchers at NTNU, Leiden University, and MIT developed a real-time calibration method that monitors qubits and continuously adjusts their frequency to counter environmental disturbances. The technique, dubbed “Binary-Search Hamiltonian Tracking,” uses an FPGA controller to extend qubit lifetime and enhance precision. Jacob Benestad, the lead researcher, compared it to “tuning a guitar string while it’s being played.”

IBM announced that conventional AMD processors can execute a key quantum error correction algorithm, suggesting that existing classical hardware may accelerate progress toward fault-tolerant systems by offloading error correction workloads.

At the Q2B25 conference in Paris, experts highlighted progress in quantum error correction codes and decoders. Panelists discussed concatenated codes, directional codes, and IBM’s bivariate bicycle codes. The discussion emphasized the target of achieving 1 million error-free quantum operations (MegaQuOp) and eventually 1 trillion (TeraQuOp), compared to current systems that manage only a few hundred operations before errors occur. The panel also noted that trapped-ion and neutral-atom platforms are approximately 1,000 times slower than superconducting and photonic qubits, creating trade-offs between speed and error rates.

Bridging Worlds: NVQLink and Hybrid Systems

NVIDIA’s announcement of NVQLink on October 28 represents a major infrastructure development. The open system architecture enables tight coupling between GPU supercomputers and quantum processors (QPUs). Seventeen quantum hardware builders , five controller builders, and nine U.S. national laboratories are involved in the initiative.

The QPU builders include Alice & Bob, Anyon Computing, Atom Computing, Diraq, Infleqtion, IonQ, IQM Quantum Computers, ORCA Computing, Oxford Quantum Circuits, Pasqal, Quandela, Quantinuum, Quantum Circuits Inc., Quantum Machines, Quantum Motion, QuEra, and Rigetti. Controller builders include Keysight Technologies, Qblox, QubiC, and Zurich Instruments. The participating national labs are Brookhaven, Fermilab, Lawrence Berkeley, Los Alamos, MIT Lincoln Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Pacific Northwest, Sandia, and Argonne.

NVQLink addresses a critical requirement for fault-tolerant quantum computing: error correction demands hybrid quantum-classical systems with extremely low latency. Alice & Bob , which uses cat qubits that it claims reduce hardware requirements by 200 times compared to competing approaches, will integrate NVQLink for GPU compilation, live decoding, and dynamic calibration. Infleqtion announced integration with its neutral-atom Sqale quantum computer, providing a standardized, low-latency connection for real-time hybrid computing.

Berkeley Lab partnered with NVIDIA to use its open-source QubiC platform to combine QPUs, GPUs, and CPUs for quantum error correction and hybrid algorithms. NVIDIA also revealed plans to deploy two AI-ready supercomputers, Solstice (with 100,000 Blackwell GPUs) and Equinox (with 10,000 Blackwell GPUs), at Argonne National Laboratory in 2026.

The hybrid approach is taking shape beyond NVIDIA as well. Saudi Aramco launched a quantum emulator designed to simulate quantum systems using classical computing resources, enabling researchers to test quantum algorithms before quantum hardware is available. The emulator aims to accelerate quantum research in energy applications.

Industry Movements

Consolidation

Google acquired Atlantic Quantum on October 2, absorbing the MIT-founded startup’s modular chip stack technology and team. Atlantic Quantum had developed an approach integrating qubits and control electronics in the same cold stage, aiming to streamline hardware and enhance scalability. The acquisition brings co-founders Bharath Kannan (CEO), Simon Gustavsson (CTO), Will Oliver, Jonas Bylander, Tim Menke, Youngkyu Sung, Leon Ding, and Shereen Shermak into Google Quantum AI. This reflects a broader trend of research-intensive startups being absorbed into larger corporate quantum programs.

Commercial Deployments

D-Wave signed a 10 million agreement with Swiss Quantum Technology SA to deploy an Advantage2 annealing quantum computer in Europe. The system features over 4,400 qubits and will be accessible via D-Wave’s Leap cloud service. SQT will have 50% access to the system for five years, supporting the newly launched Q-Alliance in Italy. The deployment aims to advance quantum computing research while addressing energy efficiency concerns.

IBM inaugurated the IBM Quantum System Two with a 156-qubit Heron processor in San Sebastian, Spain - the first such system in Europe and third globally. The Basque regional government invested 50 million ($58 million) in the facility. The Heron processor delivers 50 times increased capability, 16 times increased precision, and 25 times increased speed compared to previous systems. IBM’s quantum network now includes 700,000 developers. The center aims to reach “quantum utility” by 2026.

China launched a commercial superconducting quantum computer based on the Zuchongzhi 3.0 design, offering remote access via the Tianyan quantum cloud platform. Built by China Telecom Quantum Group and QuantumCTek, the system features a 105-qubit chip with 182 couplers. The Tianyan platform hosts an 880-qubit superconducting cluster across multiple 24-qubit and 176-qubit machines. The platform has received 37 million visits from users in 60 countries and has handled 2 million experiments since its November 2023 launch.

Quandela delivered “Lucy,” a 12-qubit universal digital photonic quantum computer, to CEA’s TGCC for the EuroHPC and GENCI consortium. The system will be coupled with the Joliot-Curie supercomputer and made accessible to European researchers starting in 2026. Notably, 80% of components are sourced within Europe, marking a step toward technological sovereignty. CEO Niccolo Somaschi noted the system took 12 months to assemble at Quandela’s facilities.

Technology Roadmaps

PsiQuantum announced plans to build a quantum supercomputer using light-based qubits, with a goal of scaling to one million qubits. The company has taken delivery of a cryogenic cabinet for the system at its new facility in Milpitas, California. The photonic approach aims to leverage existing semiconductor manufacturing for scalability.

Research Notes

Fundamentals

Three physicists won the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics for demonstrating quantum physics at the macroscopic scale through groundbreaking quantum-tunnelling experiments. The recognition highlights progress in showing quantum effects in larger systems than previously observed.

Researchers built a “quantum lie detector” using a 73-qubit superconducting quantum processor to achieve an energy state impossible under classical physics. The result was verified to 48 standard deviations below the classical minimum, certifying nonlocal correlations in groups of up to 24 qubits. The Bell test, performed by researchers at Leiden University, Tsinghua University, and Zhejiang University, proves the system operates according to quantum principles rather than classical approximations.

A Federal Reserve study warned that quantum computers pose a “harvest now, decrypt later” threat to Bitcoin and other blockchains. Encrypted data collected today could be decrypted in the future, exposing transaction histories and private keys. The study notes that even post-quantum cryptography cannot protect already harvested data. Federal agencies have been directed to begin migration to post-quantum cryptography by 2035.

Materials and Hardware

Penn State researchers developed strained barium titanate thin films (40 nanometers thick) that improve electron-to-photon conversion by over 10 times at cryogenic temperatures. The material, first discovered in 1941, could advance quantum networks and make data centers more energy efficient by enabling better microwave-to-optical conversion for quantum communications.

University of Chicago scientists developed molecular qubits made with erbium that are compatible with standard telecommunications wavelengths and silicon photonics. Published in Science, the research creates a nanoscale bridge between magnetic spin states and light, enabling potential quantum networks that integrate with existing optical fiber infrastructure. The work involved collaboration with UC Berkeley, Argonne National Laboratory, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Harvard researchers demonstrated continuous operation of a quantum processor, an important step toward practical quantum computers that can run sustained calculations rather than single-shot experiments. The advance addresses the need for quantum systems to maintain coherence over extended computation periods.

Algorithms and Applications

University at Buffalo researchers expanded the truncated Wigner approximation (TWA), enabling quantum simulations that once required supercomputers to run on regular laptops. The user-friendly framework allows physicists to set up and run simulations in days rather than dealing with pages of complex mathematics. The study was published in PRX Quantum in September 2025.

Researchers applied quantum computing approaches to quantum chemistry simulations and optimization problems, demonstrating progress toward practical applications. The work includes methods for simulating molecular systems and solving combinatorial optimization problems using quantum algorithms.

A study explored the fundamental limits of quantum computation, examining what types of problems quantum computers can and cannot solve efficiently. The research provides theoretical bounds on quantum advantage and helps distinguish between problems that benefit from quantum speedup and those that do not.

What This Month Means

The October developments show quantum computing progressing on multiple parallel tracks. The 6,100-qubit milestone demonstrates that neutral-atom platforms can scale without sacrificing coherence, challenging the assumption that qubit count and stability are fundamentally opposed. Google’s verifiable quantum advantage claim, while met with appropriate skepticism, represents progress toward demonstrating computations that classical systems cannot efficiently verify or perform.

The error correction advances - AFT’s 10-100x overhead reduction, IonQ’s 99.99% gate fidelity, and real-time calibration methods - directly address the primary obstacle to fault-tolerant quantum computing. These are incremental but measurable steps toward systems that can perform long, reliable computations.

NVQLink signals a broader industry shift toward hybrid quantum-classical architectures. With 17 quantum hardware builders and 9 national labs committing to the standard, the field is converging on a model where GPUs handle error correction, control, and data processing while QPUs execute quantum operations. This division of labor may accelerate progress by letting each platform do what it does best.

The industry movements - acquisitions, deployments, and new commercial systems - reflect growing confidence that quantum computing will eventually become practical. The competitive landscape is intensifying globally, with the U.S., Europe, and China each making strategic investments in quantum infrastructure.

The field is transitioning from “can we build it?” to “can we make it useful?” The timeline remains long - fault-tolerant quantum computers capable of solving commercially valuable problems are still years away. But progress is measurable across hardware, error correction, and system integration.

This comprehensive review covers 4 articles published between September 11-24, 2025, surveying significant advances in materials discovery. Scientists achieved record-breaking atomic resolution to directly observe phasons–a theoretical vibration predicted decades ago–while MIT and Google DeepMind unveiled an AI tool that generates 80% more stable quantum materials. These breakthroughs in observation and design mark September as a month of substantial progress in materials discovery.

The Big Story: Imaging the Unseeable

For the first time, scientists have directly imaged phasons –a type of atomic vibration predicted by theorists decades ago but never observed directly until now.

Researchers at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign achieved this using electron ptychography , an advanced imaging technique that reached a resolution of 15 picometers (0.2 angstroms). This sub-atomic resolution is necessary because phasons involve extremely subtle atomic motion–the heat-induced jiggling amounts to only about 0.05 angstroms.

The team, led by Professor Pinshane Huang and postdoctoral researcher Yichao Zhang , studied twisted bilayers of tungsten diselenide (WSe₂) . In these moiré superlattices, they could observe how phasons vary with atomic arrangement and how they contribute to heat transfer at the atomic level.

The research, published in Science , reconciles theoretical predictions with direct observation. It opens new paths to control heat transfer in 2D materials, which could enable more efficient electronics and better thermal management in quantum computing hardware.

New Tools: AI Designs Stable Materials

While scientists push the boundaries of observation, others are revolutionizing how materials are designed. A collaboration between MIT and Google DeepMind has produced SCIGEN , an AI tool that generates materials that actually exist in the physical world.

The problem with generative AI for materials design is that unconstrained models frequently output structures that are physically impossible or unstable. SCIGEN addresses this by incorporating geometric and physical constraints directly into the generation process.

In trials, the approach produced 80% more stable structures than unconstrained models. The tool targets applications in quantum computing, energy storage, and electronics . Researchers Tianyu Zhu of MIT and Ekin Dogus Cubuk of Google DeepMind led the development.

SCIGEN joins other efforts like Microsoft’s MatterGen in bridging AI creativity with physical reality. However, challenges around scaling and experimental validation remain before these AI-designed materials can move from simulation to laboratory.

Quantum Materials Advance

In industry news, IonQ announced a breakthrough in synthetic diamond materials that accelerates the scale and production of quantum networking. Synthetic diamonds are crucial for quantum communication infrastructure, where they serve as hosts for nitrogen-vacancy centers that can store and transmit quantum information. The advancement addresses material limitations that have constrained quantum network deployment and could enable larger, more efficient quantum networks.

Perspective: Serendipity and Scale

The gap between discovery and mass production is a theme that runs through materials science. Few understand this better than Sumio Iijima , the researcher who discovered carbon nanotubes in 1991 .

In a recent interview, Iijima–now a Senior Research Fellow at NEC Corporation with positions at Meijo University, the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, and Nagoya University–reflected on two problems he’s tackling. One is solving a crystal structure for solid-state lithium-ion batteries. The other is the mass production challenge for carbon nanotubes .

Iijima has spent two years working on the alignment problem . Solving it would allow carbon nanotubes to replace silicon in semiconductors and transistors, potentially transforming electronics. He emphasizes the close link between pure and applied research, noting that serendipity plays a crucial role in scientific discovery–the oxide he studied 40 to 50 years ago is now used as an electrode material in solid-state batteries.

The scale of equipment needed for this work underscores the challenge. An electron microscope costs approximately 500 million yen , while a neutron diffraction facility runs about 10 billion yen . Despite these obstacles, Iijima remains optimistic about the field’s future.

Looking Ahead

These four stories trace the materials discovery pipeline from observation to design to manufacturing. Better observation tools–like the 15 picometer resolution achieved through electron ptychography–reveal phenomena that were previously theoretical. Better design tools–like constrained generative AI–create viable materials faster than trial-and-error experimentation. Better manufacturing methods–like synthetic diamond production and carbon nanotube scaling–bring discoveries from the lab to the real world.

The trend is clear: tools are becoming more precise and more predictive. The bottleneck is shifting from discovery itself to validation and scale. As Iijima’s reflection reminds us, the time between discovering a material and mass-producing it can span decades. The advances of September 2025 suggest that timeline may be shortening.
