This month, researchers deployed transformer models to predict alloy properties, LLMs to design molecules, and autonomous labs to accelerate discovery. Meanwhile, a surprising finding revealed billions in rare earth elements hiding in coal ash waste.

This comprehensive review covers 18 articles published in April 2025, surveying the latest advances at the intersection of AI and materials discovery.

The Big Story: AI Models Scale Materials Discovery

Transformer architectures, originally developed for natural language processing, are now demonstrating their value in materials science. Researchers at the University of North Texas applied a transformer-based language model to predict mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The approach addresses the perennial challenge of data scarcity in materials science through pre-training on synthetic data followed by fine-tuning on experimental HEA datasets. The model outperformed traditional regression methods including random forests, Gaussian processes, gradient boosting, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbors, artificial neural networks, deep neural networks, and convolutional neural networks.

The transformer architecture offers an additional advantage: interpretability through attention weight visualization, allowing researchers to understand which features drive predictions. This transparency is valuable for materials scientists who need to understand the physical basis of model predictions.

MIT researchers introduced Llamole, a multimodal AI system that combines large language models with graph-based molecular representations for synthesis planning . The approach improved synthesis planning success rates from 5% to 35% compared to baseline methods. The system uses contrastive learning to align molecular graphs with text descriptions, enabling the LLM to reason about chemical structures more effectively. While 35% may seem modest, it represents a seven-fold improvement over conventional approaches.

Two papers in Science on April 4 highlighted complementary AI-driven approaches. Researchers at the University of Toronto demonstrated that active learning combined with domain adaptation accelerates the discovery of advanced oxygen evolution electrocatalysts for water splitting. By strategically selecting experiments and adapting models across related domains, the approach reduces the experimental burden of discovering efficient electrocatalysts.

Separately, a high-throughput experimentation platform published in Science Advances enables rapid screening and optimization of electrochemical processes. The platform facilitates accelerated materials discovery through automated, data-driven methods that can handle large numbers of experiments in parallel.

For organic photovoltaics, researchers developed a machine learning framework using polymer-unit fingerprints (PUFp) with a random forest algorithm. The PUFp representation outperformed traditional MACCS fingerprints for predicting power conversion efficiency. The database includes 1,343 experimentally validated OPV non-fullerene acceptor materials and 260 donor materials, providing a substantial foundation for training predictive models. The PUFp system uses 413 different polymer units for N-type OPVs and 209 for P-type OPVs, compared to the 166 digital keys in MACCS fingerprints.

Method Application Key Advantage Source
Transformer models High-entropy alloys Outperforms RF and GP Nature
LLMs + Graph models Molecular design 35% vs 5% success MIT News
Active learning Electrocatalysts Efficient discovery Science
Random forest + PUFp Organic PV Better than MACCS Nature

These developments represent a broader trend of scaling AI architectures from their original domains into materials science, bringing with them new capabilities for handling complex, high-dimensional materials data.

Self-Driving Labs: From Vision to Infrastructure

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are transitioning from conceptual frameworks to operational research infrastructure. A perspective article in Nature articulates two distinct paradigms for democratizing SDL-assisted research: centralized facilities and distributed networks of open-source tools.

The centralized model, exemplified by facilities like CERN, provides access to sophisticated equipment that individual labs could not afford. The distributed model, drawing inspiration from projects like Galaxy Zoo and Foldit, leverages networks of researchers and open-source tools to spread access more broadly. The article highlights several enabling technologies including Chemspyd, PyLabRobot, PerQueue, and Jubilee that provide building blocks for constructing autonomous laboratory systems.

According to the perspective, SDLs address two critical bottlenecks in materials discovery: the pace of experimentation and the accessibility of advanced equipment. By automating experiment design and execution, these systems can tackle grand challenges that would be impractical for human-operated labs.

Concrete examples of autonomous labs in action are emerging in photonics research. An article in Optics & Photonics News describes real-world implementations of self-driving labs for optical materials discovery. These systems combine automated synthesis platforms with in-line characterization and closed-loop optimization, enabling researchers to explore materials spaces more thoroughly than manual methods allow.

The democratization angle is significant. While high-throughput facilities have existed for decades, the emergence of modular, open-source SDL components could allow smaller research groups to build autonomous capabilities tailored to their specific needs. This could broaden participation in advanced materials research beyond well-funded institutions.

Centralized vs. Distributed Models

The Nature perspective distinguishes between facility-based SDLs, which concentrate resources and expertise, and distributed networks that leverage collaboration and shared software. Each approach has trade-offs: centralized facilities offer specialized equipment and staff support, while distributed models provide broader access and flexibility.

Real-World Implementations

The Optics & Photonics article highlights working SDLs that demonstrate the practical benefits of autonomous experimentation, including accelerated discovery cycles and the ability to run experiments continuously without human intervention.

Industrial Adoption and Infrastructure

Commercialization and infrastructure investments accelerated in April, signaling growing industry confidence in AI-driven materials discovery approaches.

Product Launch: SES AI’s Molecular Universe

SES AI Corporation launched Molecular Universe MU-0, a battery material discovery platform powered by physics and AI. The platform features an interactive map of small molecules embedded in a 512-dimensional space using UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection). This high-dimensional representation captures complex molecular relationships that can guide the discovery of new battery materials.

The platform has already attracted two signed OEM customers, according to SES AI Founder and CEO Qichao Hu . A live demo was scheduled for April 29, 2025. Founded in 2012, SES AI is positioning MU-0 as a tool to accelerate next-generation battery development for both Li-Metal and Li-ion chemistries.

Partnership: Microsoft and Johns Hopkins

Microsoft and the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory entered a strategic collaboration to advance robotics and materials discovery using AI. The partnership focuses on two areas: developing autonomous robot teaming systems with generative AI for disaster and battlefield scenarios, and testing Microsoft’s MatterGen model for materials discovery aimed at extreme environments.

The collaboration aims to enhance capabilities for scenarios where human presence is risky or impractical, combining APL’s domain expertise with Microsoft’s AI infrastructure. MatterGen, Microsoft’s generative model for materials design, will be tested on materials discovery problems relevant to extreme environment applications.

Infrastructure: UK Semiconductor Investment

The University of Sheffield received £7 million to establish an AI-driven molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) system for semiconductor materials discovery. The system will use AI to control crystal growth at the atomic level, enabling the discovery of new semiconductor materials with tailored properties.

This investment represents a national capability for the UK, providing researchers with access to advanced synthesis equipment enhanced by AI control. The MBE approach allows precise deposition of materials layer by layer, and AI optimization could accelerate the discovery of materials for quantum computing, photonics, and other advanced applications.

Initiative Amount Focus Impact
UK MBE System £7M Semiconductors National capability
SES AI MU-0 Undisclosed Battery materials Commercial platform
Microsoft-JHU Strategic Robotics + Materials Extreme environments

According to a StartUs Insights industry report , these developments are part of a broader trend of industry adoption of AI for materials discovery, with companies investing in both internal capabilities and external partnerships.

Unexpected Discoveries

Billions in Rare Earths Found in Coal Ash

Researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin discovered that coal ash waste contains significant quantities of rare earth elements. The study estimates 11 million tons of rare earth elements in U.S. coal ash, compared to 1.4 million tons in conventional sources. At current market values, this represents approximately $8.4 billion worth of critical materials.

The finding challenges the conventional view of coal ash as purely waste material. According to study authors Davin Bagdonas and Bridget Scanlon , the widespread availability of coal ash across the U.S. could reduce dependency on foreign sources, which currently dominate the market. The Asia Pacific region accounted for 86.14% of the rare earth market in 2023.

Chris Young , chief strategy officer at ElementUSA, noted that extracting rare earths from coal ash could have lower environmental impact than conventional mining. The global rare earth market was valued at $3.74 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $8.14 billion by 2032, driven by demand for clean technologies.

Thermodynamics-Defying Materials for EV Restoration

University of Chicago scientists discovered materials that appear to defy conventional thermodynamics, exhibiting properties that could enable the restoration of degraded EV batteries. The materials, which include metastable compounds with negative thermal expansion, maintain their structure under conditions that would typically cause decomposition.

These anomalous materials challenge the understanding of stability in solid-state systems and could provide new pathways for battery recycling and rejuvenation. The research suggests that certain materials can exist in states that thermodynamic calculations would predict to be unstable, opening new possibilities for energy storage applications.

Car Exhaust Improves Catalyst Performance

In a serendipitous discovery at Washington State University , researchers found that exposing certain catalysts to car exhaust gases actually improved their performance. The unexpected result emerged during experiments designed to study catalyst degradation under realistic conditions.

The researchers discovered that specific components of exhaust, including carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons, can modify catalyst surfaces in ways that enhance activity for certain reactions. This counterintuitive finding could lead to new catalyst treatment methods that improve efficiency for emission control and chemical synthesis applications.

Hidden Quantum States in Twisted Materials

A Japan-US collaboration revealed hidden quantum states in twisted bilayer materials that were not predicted by conventional theory. The discovery involved creating previously unobserved twist angle configurations and measuring their electronic properties.

The exotic states emerge from the moiré patterns created when two-dimensional materials are twisted relative to each other. These findings expand the understanding of quantum phenomena in layered materials and could inform the design of materials for quantum computing and advanced electronics.

Hydrogel Reprograms Cancer Cells

Researchers at Hokkaido University discovered that a specific double-network hydrogel can rapidly reprogram fully differentiated cancer cells into cancer stem cells (CSCs) through a process they call HARP (hydrogel-activated reprogramming phenomenon). Within 24 hours, cancer cells form CSC spheres on the hydrogel surface.

Cancer stem cells are typically extremely rare, occurring at approximately 1 in a million cells in a tumor, making them difficult to study. The ability to generate large quantities of CSCs in the lab accelerates research into therapies that target these treatment-resistant cells, which are believed to drive cancer recurrence. According to Professor Shinya Tanaka , this approach could enable personalized medicine approaches and novel drug screening platforms.

Looking Ahead

The convergence of several trends suggests that AI-driven materials discovery is moving from experimental approach to established practice. Nature Computational Science launched a collection on generative models for molecular design and discovery, signaling the field’s maturation. The collection highlights approaches including variational autoencoders, diffusion models, and large language models for navigating the vast theoretical chemical space, which contains an estimated \(10^{60}\) feasible compounds.

Kristin Persson , founder of the Materials Project, noted that the combination of high-quality data and machine learning is transforming how researchers approach materials discovery. In an interview with the Department of Energy, she emphasized that data-driven methods allow researchers to explore chemical spaces more systematically than traditional trial-and-error approaches.

The direction of travel points toward solving major challenges. A Scientific American analysis examined how new materials could ease climate impacts, highlighting the role of AI in accelerating the discovery of materials for clean energy, carbon capture, and sustainable infrastructure.

The pattern is clear: AI architectures are scaling to handle more complex materials problems, self-driving labs are democratizing access to automated experimentation, and industry is investing in infrastructure to bring these advances from lab to market. The unexpected discoveries—from rare earths in coal ash to thermodynamics-defying materials—remind us that materials science still holds the capacity for surprise, even as computational methods make exploration more systematic.

This comprehensive review covers 185 articles published in April 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing. This month brought remarkable progress in quantum reliability: Alice & Bob demonstrated cat qubits with 160x fewer errors , while researchers unveiled the first comprehensive benchmark showing quantum systems surpassing classical simulation limits. Beyond the lab, governments committed hundreds of millions, and new quantum systems came online worldwide.

Reliability Breakthrough: Cat Qubits Get 160x Better

The most significant technical advance this month came from Alice & Bob, which achieved a 160x reduction in bit-flip errors using “squeezed” cat qubits. The technique extends cat qubit lifetime from 138 milliseconds to 22 seconds—a dramatic improvement that makes error correction considerably less resource-intensive. Bit-flip errors, where a qubit spontaneously flips from \(|0\rangle\) to \(|1\rangle\), are one of the two fundamental error types in quantum computing. Suppressing them at the hardware level reduces the overhead required for software-based error correction.

The squeezing technique works without modifying circuit design, making it potentially applicable to existing cat qubit architectures. Cat qubits are a type of bosonic code that encodes quantum information in the oscillations of a superconducting resonator, named after Schrodinger’s famous thought experiment. By squeezing the quantum state, the researchers effectively narrowed the uncertainty in one quadrature while expanding it in the orthogonal direction—trading one type of error for another that’s easier to correct.

Complementary Error Correction Advances

Alice & Bob’s breakthrough is part of a broader set of error correction advances this month:

  • University of Twente researchers invented a photonic error correction method that filters high-quality photons at the source rather than correcting errors after the fact. Previous approaches required hundreds of physical photons to create a single reliable logical qubit; the new technique dramatically reduces this overhead, making photonic quantum computers cheaper and more practical.

  • Scientists at the University of Witwatersrand developed optical skyrmions —topological structures formed in entangled photon pairs that encode quantum information in their global properties rather than local states. Even when entanglement degrades, the topological protection helps preserve information, potentially enabling more robust quantum networks.

  • Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory researchers reduced superinductor capacitance by over 60% through a new chemical etching process that suspends superinductors above the wafer surface. This cuts substrate-related noise, a major source of error in superconducting qubits, and provides a practical fabrication method for scaling up.

  • UCL engineers broke a 25-year barrier in chip fabrication by using arsenic atoms instead of phosphorus for single-atom placement. They achieved 97% accuracy in positioning individual atoms—compared to the 70% success rate typical for phosphorus—demonstrating a path toward near-zero failure rates in quantum chip manufacturing.

These advances represent complementary approaches to the same fundamental challenge: making quantum computations reliable enough to be useful. While each targets different qubit modalities—superconducting, photonic, topological, silicon-based—together they indicate rapid progress across the field.

Measuring Progress: When Do Quantum Computers Win?

A critical development this month came from the Jülich Research Centre, which unveiled a comprehensive benchmark comparing 19 quantum processing units from five suppliers (IBM, Quantinuum, IonQ, Rigetti, and IQM). Built around the MaxCut optimization problem, the benchmark provides a platform-agnostic way to measure quantum performance as systems scale.

The results revealed important differences between platforms. Quantinuum’s H2-1 passed the benchmark at 56 qubits—a scale that surpasses exact classical simulation. The test used 4,620 two-qubit gates in a Linear Ramp Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (LR-QAOA) circuit, demonstrating that trapped-ion systems can maintain coherence at useful scales.

IBM’s processors showed different strengths: the Fez chip handled 100-qubit problems at depths up to 10,000 layers, though coherent information was retained only through approximately 300 layers. More importantly, the newer Marrakesh chip demonstrated half the error rate per layered gate compared to Fez, showing rapid iterative improvement in IBM’s superconducting hardware.

Benchmarking Software Performance

Separately, researchers introduced Benchpress, an open-source benchmarking suite for quantum software development kits. The suite includes 1,066 tests covering circuit construction, manipulation, and compilation across SDKs including Qiskit, Cirq, Braket, Tket, and others. In initial tests, Qiskit completed circuit construction tests in 2.0 seconds while Tket required 14.2 seconds—but Tket produced circuits with fewer two-qubit gates for certain decompositions, highlighting different performance tradeoffs.

The Challenge of Meaningful Benchmarks

The quest for meaningful benchmarks also revealed ongoing controversies. IEEE Spectrum published a critique of D-Wave’s quantum supremacy claims , noting that the company’s annealing approach solves different problems than gate-based quantum computers and that direct comparisons are often misleading. New Scientist similarly examined why quantum computers continue to fail certain key tests, emphasizing that cross-entropy benchmarking—while useful for measuring random circuit sampling—may not capture performance on practical applications.

This tension between demonstrating raw quantum advantage and solving useful problems remains central to the field. The MaxCut benchmark represents progress because it’s based on a real optimization problem with commercial applications, rather than an artificial benchmark designed solely to showcase quantum speedups.

Building the Quantum Internet: QNodeOS and Distributed Computing

Quantum Operating System

Researchers unveiled QNodeOS, billed as the world’s first operating system for quantum computers . The system enables multiple quantum computers to be controlled centrally and connected for distributed quantum computing—a foundational capability for a future quantum internet. QNodeOS handles resource allocation, job scheduling, and network management across diverse quantum hardware, abstracting away the differences between systems from different vendors.

Network Infrastructure

The UK demonstrated a 410-kilometer quantum network integrating both quantum key distribution (QKD) and entanglement distribution . The network connects multiple nodes and represents a step toward practical quantum communication infrastructure. Simultaneously, the UK launched its Integrated Quantum Networks Hub at Heriot-Watt University, bringing together academia and industry to pioneer secure quantum networks .

In the United States, IonQ and the Electric Power Board (EPB) launched a $22 million Quantum Innovation Center in Chattanooga, Tennessee. The center will house IonQ quantum computing systems and establish the first U.S. hub dedicated to quantum computing and networking research.

New Deployments

IQM announced it will install Poland’s first superconducting quantum computer at Wroclaw University of Science and Technology. The system will support Polish research in quantum algorithms and materials science.

Hardware Milestones: New Systems Come Online

Japan

Fujitsu and RIKEN unveiled a 256-qubit superconducting quantum computer , quadrupling the qubit count of their previous 64-qubit system. The new system builds on Fujitsu’s ongoing collaboration with RIKEN and represents a significant step toward Japan’s goal of developing a domestically produced quantum computing stack.

Separately, ULVAC delivered a cryogenic system for Japan’s first fully domestic quantum computer , supporting the country’s push for end-to-end sovereign quantum capabilities.

India

QpiAI launched the QpiAI-Indus, India’s first full-stack 25-qubit quantum computer under the country’s National Quantum Mission. The system features superconducting qubits and includes both cloud access and on-premises deployment options. India’s quantum push has gained momentum following a government commitment of approximately $1 billion over five years.

Europe

Beyond the IQM deployment in Poland, several European quantum initiatives advanced this month. The UK’s quantum hubs continued their work on networking and applications, while Norway announced new investment in quantum technology research .

Mobile Systems

SaxonQ demonstrated applications running on a mobile quantum computer powered by Quantum Machines’ control electronics. The demonstration showed that room-temperature quantum computing—using nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond—can operate outside specialized data center environments, opening possibilities for field-deployed quantum sensors and computers.

Company/Organization Qubits Technology Location Status
Fujitsu-RIKEN 256 Superconducting Japan Operational
QpiAI 25 Superconducting India Launched
IQM Not specified Superconducting Poland (WUST) Announced
SaxonQ Not specified NV Center (room temp) Mobile Demonstrated

Research Highlights: From Quasiparticles to Topology

Mathematical Applications

Researchers used Quantinuum’s H2-2 quantum computer to explore knot theory , demonstrating how quantum systems can solve complex mathematical problems. The work involved implementing quantum algorithms to compute knot invariants—mathematical quantities that distinguish different types of knots—with potential applications in topological quantum computing and quantum field theory.

In a separate study, researchers demonstrated quantum computing for contingency analysis in power systems , showing how quantum algorithms could identify potentially dangerous configurations in electrical grids more efficiently than classical methods.

Physics Discoveries

National Science Foundation-funded researchers discovered a new quantum quasiparticle : fractional excitons, which carry fractions of an electron’s charge and could enable new approaches to quantum information storage and manipulation.

Researchers observed a superradiant phase transition that had been predicted for 50 years but never seen until now. The phenomenon, observed in a trapped-ion quantum simulator, could advance our understanding of open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics.

Quantinuum’s H2 system was used to simulate quantum magnetism using digital quantum simulation techniques, providing insights into magnetic materials that are difficult to study classically.

Hardware Advances

Trapped ion systems achieved a milestone in mid-circuit measurement and reset , capabilities essential for error correction and algorithm efficiency. The ability to measure qubits mid-computation without disturbing neighboring qubits, then reset and reuse them, dramatically reduces the qubit overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Practical Applications

Google Quantum AI published research on practical applications of its quantum computers , emphasizing work toward quantum advantage in materials simulation and optimization problems.

Researchers demonstrated quantum machine learning for predicting proton affinity , achieving superior accuracy compared to classical methods. Proton affinity is a key property in chemistry and drug discovery, with applications ranging from catalyst design to understanding biochemical reactions.

In China, researchers demonstrated quantum-assisted fine-tuning of billion-parameter AI models , illustrating the convergence of quantum computing and artificial intelligence—a trend that accelerated throughout 2025.

Government Bets: DARPA, UK, and Global Investment

DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative

The U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) made significant moves in quantum computing this month. The agency’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI) selected 18 companies for Stage A awards of approximately $1 million each. The winners include:

  • Atom Computing — Selected for neutral atom quantum computing exploration
  • IonQ — Selected to advance utility-scale quantum computing

The program targets utility-scale quantum systems by 2033 , with DARPA taking an agnostic approach to qubit modalities. Stage A requires companies to develop conceptual descriptions of how they would achieve a logical qubit error rate of \(10^{-6}\) or better—a threshold considered necessary for practical quantum advantage.

UK Quantum Investment

The UK government announced £121 million in funding for quantum applications in fraud detection, anti-money laundering, and cybersecurity . The investment targets practical applications where quantum computing could provide near-term value, though some analysts questioned whether the amount is sufficient given the scale of the challenge.

Other Government Initiatives

  • Norway announced new investment in quantum technology research , strengthening its national quantum capabilities.
  • Colorado received a $40.5 million federal grant for quantum technology development, solidifying the state’s position as a U.S. quantum hub.
  • Italy finalized its national quantum strategy , positioning the country to compete in the European quantum ecosystem.
  • The EU explored quantum computing applications in the energy sector, examining how quantum algorithms could optimize power grids .
  • National security concerns gained prominence, with analyses of quantum threats to nuclear command and control systems and the UK’s quantum security posture .
Country/Region Investment Focus Areas Timeline
USA (DARPA) ~$18M (Stage A) Utility-scale systems, benchmarking Target: 2033
UK £121M Fraud detection, AML, cybersecurity Immediate deployment
Norway Not specified Quantum research infrastructure Ongoing
Colorado (USA) $40.5M Quantum tech development hub Multi-year
Italy Not specified National quantum strategy Strategic framework

Industry and Partnerships: Quantum Goes Commercial

Healthcare & Research Partnerships

CAS (a division of the American Chemical Society) and Cleveland Clinic formed a strategic collaboration to advance brain health research using AI and quantum computing. The partnership aims to shorten the typical 17-year timeline from lab discovery to approved therapy, with initial projects focusing on Alzheimer’s drug discovery.

The Milner Therapeutics Institute at Cambridge University signed an MOU with Yonsei University to foster joint quantum computing research. Yonsei will utilize Korea’s first IBM Quantum Computer for collaborative projects, aiming to synergize quantum computing with AI-driven drug discovery.

Investments & Funding

  • BTQ Technologies signed a term sheet to invest €2 million in QPerfect , a neutral atom quantum computing company. The investment grants BTQ a 16.67% equity stake with an option for full ownership within 12 months. QPerfect’s MIMIQ platform provides quantum design automation and simulation capabilities.

  • Rigetti Computing closed a $35 million strategic investment from Quanta Computer, finalizing the investment portion of their collaboration agreement. The partnership aims to combine Quanta’s manufacturing expertise with Rigetti’s superconducting quantum technology.

  • IQM, the Finnish quantum startup, is seeking approximately €128 million in a new funding round as the quantum computing industry sees increased investor interest.

  • IBM announced plans to spend approximately $150 billion on quantum computing over the coming decade, though analysts questioned whether the full amount represents direct quantum investment or broader computational infrastructure.

Technology Partnerships

  • Quantum Machines partnered with NVIDIA’s Accelerated Quantum Research Center to integrate quantum processors with AI supercomputers . The collaboration will use NVIDIA’s GB200 Grace Blackwell Superchips and QM’s OPX1000 control system to enhance quantum-classical communication.

  • Fujitsu expanded its quantum collaboration with RIKEN following the unveiling of their 256-qubit system, strengthening Japan’s domestic quantum capabilities.

  • Terra Quantum announced a strategic partnership with Siemens , targeting quantum applications in industrial optimization and sensing.

  • IonQ expanded its quantum collaboration in Japan through a memorandum of understanding with AIST (National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology), strengthening the company’s presence in the Asian market.

Government Contracts

  • Quantum Computing Inc. (QCi) was awarded a contract to support NASA’s space-based lidar data analysis , applying quantum algorithms to Earth observation data.

  • A UK consortium received a £4.7 million award targeting fault-tolerant quantum computing , accelerating research toward error-corrected quantum systems.

Industry Trends: Market Growth, AI Convergence, and Realistic Expectations

Market Projections

The quantum computing market is projected to reach $2.2 billion by 2027 , according to industry surveys. This growth is driven by increasing enterprise adoption, government investment, and maturing hardware platforms.

Survey data indicates that 83% of quantum professionals expect quantum utility to arrive within a decade , reflecting growing confidence in the field’s trajectory. However, expectations vary significantly by sector and application area.

Quantum-AI Convergence

The convergence of quantum computing and artificial intelligence accelerated this month. Observers noted that quantum SDKs are evolving into Quantum AI SDKs , reflecting the growing integration of quantum computing with machine learning workflows. Google in particular is exploring how quantum computing could supercharge its AI ambitions , potentially using quantum systems for training optimization or inference acceleration.

Geographic Competition

The race for quantum advantage has distinct geographic dimensions. Chicago is positioning itself as a quantum hub with $500 million in state investment , leveraging its concentration of quantum research institutions and companies. Meanwhile, the U.S.-China competition in quantum technology continues to shape national strategies and investment priorities.

Sector-Specific Applications

Industry analyses explored quantum computing’s potential across sectors:

  • Finance: Quantum computing could deliver $450-850 billion in value by 2035 , according to market projections, with applications in portfolio optimization, risk analysis, and fraud detection.

  • Supply Chains: Quantum algorithms may improve supply chain optimization by solving complex logistics problems more efficiently than classical methods.

  • Cryptography: The impact of quantum computing on cryptography continues to drive urgency around post-quantum cryptography migration.

Realistic Expectations

Nature published a cautionary perspective on quantum hype , reminding readers that progress is incremental and that many announced “breakthroughs” represent engineering milestones rather than revolutionary leaps. The article emphasized the gap between qubit counts and useful quantum advantage, noting that error correction remains the fundamental challenge.

Similarly, CNBC questioned whether Google and IBM’s bullish quantum optimism is justified , given that practical quantum advantage remains unproven for most commercial applications. The article noted that while technical progress is real, timelines for commercial viability may be longer than company PR suggests.

World Quantum Day 2025 (April 14) provided an occasion for industry reflection, with various stakeholders weighing in on the state of quantum computing . The consensus view acknowledged significant technical progress while emphasizing that the field remains in early stages.

Looking Ahead: What April 2025 Tells Us

The developments of April 2025 reveal a field making measurable, incremental progress on multiple fronts. Error correction advances—Alice & Bob’s cat qubits, photonic distillation, superinductor improvements, atomically precise fabrication—are systematically reducing the error rates that have long limited quantum computations. New benchmarks like MaxCut and Benchpress are giving us better ways to measure that progress and compare different approaches objectively.

Hardware deployments are expanding both in scale and geography. Japan’s 256-qubit system, India’s first full-stack quantum computer, and Poland’s inaugural superconducting system demonstrate that quantum computing is becoming a global endeavor. Governments are placing serious bets: DARPA’s 2033 target for utility-scale systems, the UK’s application-focused £121 million investment, and various national strategies all signal institutional commitment to quantum advantage.

The convergence with AI is accelerating, though it remains unclear whether quantum systems will provide meaningful advantages for machine learning in the near term. The finance sector continues to lead in commercial experimentation, while healthcare partnerships like CAS-Cleveland Clinic suggest quantum computing may find early applications in drug discovery and molecular simulation.

Yet challenges remain. Nature’s critique of quantum hype serves as a useful reminder that technical milestones don’t automatically translate to commercial advantage. The gap between laboratory demonstrations and reliable, scalable quantum systems is still substantial. Error correction, while improving, remains resource-intensive. And meaningful benchmarks that measure practical advantage—rather than contrived problems—are only beginning to emerge.

The pattern is clear: progress is happening, but it’s engineering-focused and cumulative rather than sudden and revolutionary. DARPA’s 2033 target for utility-scale quantum computing seems increasingly plausible given the rate of improvement in error rates and system scale. But the question remains which approach—superconducting, trapped ion, neutral atom, photonic—will reach practical utility first.

April 2025 didn’t deliver a single “breakthrough” that changed everything. Instead, it delivered something more valuable: evidence that multiple quantum computing approaches are making steady progress on the fundamental challenges that have limited the field for years. That may be less exciting than headlines promise, but it’s the reality of quantum computing in 2025—and it’s enough to keep the field moving forward.

The trend is attracting top AI talent, with an OpenAI vice president departing to launch an AI-powered materials science startup.

This comprehensive review covers 10 articles published during March 2025, surveying the latest developments in materials discovery. AI-driven autonomous labs are exploring vast chemical spaces at unprecedented scale, while researchers reported breakthrough materials from quantum dots to ultra-bright fluorescents. The trend is attracting top AI talent, with an OpenAI vice president departing to launch an AI-powered materials science startup.

The Acceleration Engine: AI and Automation in Materials Discovery

The most significant trend this month is the maturation of AI-driven autonomous laboratories that can systematically explore combinatorial spaces far beyond human capacity.

Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Chicago reported on Polybot , an AI-driven autonomous laboratory that explored nearly a million possible processing combinations for electronic polymer thin films. The system uses robotics and AI to autonomously run experiments, optimizing material properties like conductivity and coating defects. The research team has produced recipes for large-scale production and will share the collected data openly with the scientific community.

In parallel validation work, researchers from the University of Michigan and Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology demonstrated a new precursor selection method for inorganic materials synthesis. Using the Samsung ASTRAL robotic lab , they synthesized 35 target materials across 224 reactions , working with 27 elements and 28 unique precursors. The new approach achieved higher purity for 32 of the 35 materials . As the Department of Energy noted, this combination of improved precursor selection and robotic synthesis can “greatly accelerate materials discovery” and “reduce bottlenecks in manufacturing” known and predicted materials.

These demonstrations establish a clear pattern: AI-guided autonomous systems can now systematically explore chemical and materials spaces that would be impractical for manual experimentation, accelerating the path from prediction to validated material.

Performance Breakthroughs: New Materials with Quantified Gains

The acceleration in discovery tools is translating into materials with quantified performance improvements across applications.

Next-Generation Displays

Curtin University researchers, in collaboration with Shanghai University, Jilin University, the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Fudan University, and TCL Research, have developed non-toxic blue quantum dot LEDs that achieve 24.7% efficiency with a 30,000-hour operational lifetime . The ZnSeTeS quantum dots avoid heavy metals like cadmium, addressing a key environmental concern for display technology. This efficiency-lifetime combination for blue QLEDs could enable brighter, eco-friendly displays for TVs, smartphones, and VR headsets. The work was published in Nature.

Medical Imaging

Indiana University chemists reported ultra-bright fluorescent materials called SMILES that reach 30,000 brightness units - five times brighter than the team’s 2020 report. The materials achieve brightness through “supra-dancing” molecular behavior, where strategically placed atoms enable intense light emission. Potential applications include tumor labeling for cancer surgery and biological imaging. The work appears in Nature Chemistry.

Neural Interfaces

Rice University researchers, collaborating with Stanford University and the University of Cambridge, discovered that thermal processing of PEDOT:PSS beyond typical thresholds triples electrical conductivity while eliminating the need for chemical crosslinkers . The crosslinker removal addresses a potential source of toxicity, and the processed material maintains stability in water for 20 days with consistent performance. This could accelerate development of neural implants, biosensors, and neuromorphic computing devices.

Material Breakthrough Metric Application Source
ZnSeTeS Quantum Dots 24.7% efficiency , 30,000-hour lifetime Eco-friendly displays Curtin University
SMILES Fluorescents 30,000 brightness units Medical diagnostics Indiana University
PEDOT:PSS (thermally processed) 3x conductivity , no crosslinker Neural implants Rice University

The Role of Serendipity: Accidental Findings That Advance Science

Alongside systematic AI-driven approaches, serendipitous discoveries continue to advance materials science.

Heavy Element Chemistry

A research team at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory has discovered “berkelocene” , the first organometallic molecule containing berkelium . Working with just 0.3 milligrams of berkelium-249 - the element was first discovered at Berkeley Lab in 1949 - the team found that berkelium exhibits an unexpected +4 oxidation state in its organometallic form. This provides new insights into later actinide behavior, which is crucial for models related to nuclear waste storage and remediation. The work was published in Science.

Pattern Formation

UCLA researchers discovered that spiral patterns spontaneously form on germanium surfaces when chemical reactions couple with mechanical stress. The spirals emerge from a reaction-diffusion-convection process that creates instabilities at the reaction front. The researchers developed a theoretical framework explaining the pattern formation, offering a model for understanding similar processes in biological systems. The work appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

These discoveries underscore that while AI acceleration expands the scope of exploration, human observation and the ability to recognize unexpected phenomena remain essential to scientific discovery.

Quantum Sensing for Materials Characterization

A new characterization technique from Oak Ridge National Laboratory uses a nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond as both a quantum bit and a sensor to measure high-speed magnetic fluctuations in materials. The scanning NV center microscope detects spin fluctuations near phase transitions in magnetic thin films at room temperature . Led by Ben Lawrie and Yueh-Chun Wu , the work provides a nanoscale method for probing quantum materials, with potential applications in data storage, sensing, and quantum computing. The research was published in Nano Letters.

Industry Signal: AI Talent Migrates to Materials Science

The field is attracting serious talent and investment. Liam Fedus, vice president of research for post-training at OpenAI , has departed to launch an AI-powered materials science startup . OpenAI has confirmed it will invest in and collaborate with the new venture. Fedus joined OpenAI in 2022 and was promoted to vice president in 2024.

His departure reflects a broader trend: top AI researchers are moving to apply machine learning to scientific discovery. Google DeepMind introduced the GNoME materials discovery system in 2023, while Microsoft rolled out MatterGen and MatterSim for materials generation and simulation. The migration of senior AI talent to materials science signals market validation for AI-accelerated discovery approaches.

Additional Developments

The University of Liverpool’s Materials Innovation Factory is leveraging digital tools to shorten materials innovation timelines . A recent project led by Matt Reed applied materials characterization techniques to dinosaur fossil study, demonstrating how analytical tools cross disciplines. This interdisciplinary approach shows how materials science methods contribute to fields beyond traditional materials applications.

item.title: Quantum Computing in March: Supremacy Claims, Skepticism, and the Race to Scale
item.description:
March brought conflicting narratives in quantum computing: D-Wave claimed the first practical quantum supremacy demonstration, China unveiled a processor reportedly quadrillions of times faster than supercomputers, and Microsoft faced fierce criticism over its topological qubit breakthrough. Meanwhile, the industry poured billions into scaling hardware, with PsiQuantum raising $750 million and NVIDIA opening a dedicated quantum research center.

This comprehensive review covers 45 articles published in March 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing.
item.content:encoded:
March brought conflicting narratives in quantum computing: D-Wave claimed the first practical quantum supremacy demonstration, China unveiled a processor reportedly quadrillions of times faster than supercomputers, and Microsoft faced fierce criticism over its topological qubit breakthrough. Meanwhile, the industry poured billions into scaling hardware, with PsiQuantum raising $750 million and NVIDIA opening a dedicated quantum research center.

This comprehensive review covers 45 articles published in March 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing.

The Skeptical Breakthrough

In February, Microsoft unveiled Majorana 1, a quantum chip with a Topological Core architecture that theoretically enables stable and scalable qubits using topoconductors—materials that host exotic Majorana particles first theorized in 1937. The chip contains 8 topological qubits, and Microsoft says this architecture paves the way for million-qubit machines capable of solving complex problems within years.

But physicists aren’t buying it. A Nature report published March 18 documents widespread skepticism, with researchers saying the evidence is insufficient to support the claims. Henry Legg, a physicist at the University of St. Andrews, challenged the validity of a key test underlying Microsoft’s claims. Sergey Frolov, a professor at the University of Pittsburgh, called the project “unreliable” and cited a lack of established physics in Microsoft’s work.

Critics note this isn’t the first time Microsoft’s Majorana research has faced scrutiny—the company retracted a 2018 paper claiming detection of Majorana particles. The controversy echoes the field’s broader reproducibility crisis: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and Microsoft’s latest work has not convinced many experts.

At the American Physical Society’s Global Physics Summit on March 19, Chetan Nayak, a Microsoft researcher, presented new data defending the work. But hundreds of physicists attending the talk remained unconvinced, with some arguing the data looks like noise and the methods are flawed. Microsoft stands by its research and continues development, but the episode underscores the high standards required for breakthrough claims in quantum computing.

Three Supremacy Claims, Different Approaches

While Microsoft’s claims faced skepticism, three other groups announced quantum performance claims—each using different technologies, different benchmarks, and different levels of peer review.

D-Wave: First Practical Supremacy?

D-Wave published peer-reviewed results in Science showing its Advantage2 annealing quantum computer solved a materials simulation problem (a spin glass system) in minutes that would take the Frontier supercomputer approximately 1 million years to complete. This wasn’t a random benchmark—it was a practical scientific problem that researchers actually care about.

The study, led by researchers including Andrew King from D-Wave and Daniel Lidar from the University of Southern California, represents the first peer-reviewed demonstration of what the authors call “practical quantum supremacy”—solving a problem of practical significance faster than any classical computer could. The work built on D-Wave’s previous research using a reverse annealing protocol that allows the system to refine solutions iteratively.

Jared Rovny, a physicist at D-Wave, noted that the performance gap is so large that classical computers would need to improve by many orders of magnitude to compete. Annealing quantum computers like D-Wave’s are fundamentally different from gate-based systems—they excel at optimization problems rather than general-purpose computation, which explains why this result came on a practical materials science problem rather than an abstract benchmark.

China’s Zuchongzhi-3: Speedup on Random Circuits

Chinese researchers from the University of Science and Technology of China (USTC) unveiled Zuchongzhi 3.0, a 105-qubit superconducting processor that reportedly performs random circuit sampling (RCS)—a standard quantum benchmark—2 million billion times faster than the Frontier supercomputer. The results were published as a cover article in Physical Review Letters.

The processor achieved:

  • 99.90% parallel single-qubit gate fidelity
  • 99.62% parallel two-qubit gate fidelity
  • 72 microsecond coherence times
  • 182 couplers connecting the qubits in a 2D grid architecture

On the RCS benchmark with 83 qubits and 32 circuit layers, Zuchongzhi 3.0 completed the task in a few hundred seconds. The researchers estimate it would take Frontier approximately 6.4 billion years to simulate the same computation—a speedup factor of roughly \(2 \times 10^{15}\), or 15 orders of magnitude.

However, experts note this benchmark favors quantum methods by design. RCS doesn’t solve a practical problem—it’s designed to be hard for classical computers. Additionally, classical algorithms have improved dramatically since Google’s 2019 supremacy claim, with GPU-based simulations completing Google’s original task in 14 seconds. The Zuchongzhi results push the frontier further, but the practical applications remain limited.

Pan Jianwei, Zhu Xiaobo, and Chengzhi Peng led the USTC team, which has previously demonstrated quantum supremacy with both the Jiuzhang photonic systems and earlier Zuchongzhi superconducting processors.

Certified Randomness: A Provably Quantum Task

A collaboration between Quantinuum, the University of Texas at Austin, JPMorganChase, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and Argonne National Laboratory achieved something truly new: certified randomness that is provably impossible for classical computers to generate.

Using a 56-qubit Quantinuum H2 trapped-ion quantum computer, the team applied a protocol first proposed by Scott Aaronson in 2018 to generate random numbers that were then mathematically verified by classical supercomputers with a combined 1.1 exaflops of sustained performance. The team certified 71,313 bits of entropy—randomness that can be mathematically proven to be genuinely unpredictable.

The research, published in Nature on March 26, represents a practical quantum application with real-world utility. Certified randomness is crucial for:

  • Cryptography: Generating unguessable encryption keys
  • Fairness: Ensuring truly random selections in lotteries and elections
  • Privacy: Creating random numbers that cannot be predicted or manipulated

Unlike the other supremacy claims, certified randomness isn’t about speed—it’s about capability. Classical computers provably cannot generate this type of mathematically verifiable randomness, making it a fundamental demonstration of quantum advantage.

Rajeeb Hazra, CEO of Quantinuum, called the milestone “a practical application of quantum computing that is beyond the reach of classical systems.”

Company Technology Benchmark Speedup Peer Review
D-Wave Annealing (Advantage2) Spin glass simulation Minutes vs. 1M years Yes (Science)
China (USTC) Superconducting (105 qubits) Random circuit sampling \(2 \times 10^{15}\)x faster Pending (PRL)
Quantinuum + partners Trapped-ion (56 qubits) Certified randomness Classically impossible Yes (Nature)

Hardware Advances: Scaling and Error Correction

Beyond the headline-grabbing supremacy claims, March brought significant advances in quantum hardware—particularly in error correction, the bottleneck that determines whether large-scale quantum computing becomes practical.

Error Correction Breakthroughs

Fujitsu, QuTech, and TU Delft set a new world record by achieving quantum gate error rates below 0.1% using a two-qubit system built on diamond spin qubits. Some gates achieved error rates as low as 0.001%. The researchers used ultrapure synthetic diamonds from Element Six and designed quantum gates to decouple qubits from environmental noise.

This milestone is significant because error correction requires physical qubits with error rates low enough that logical qubits can be constructed with reasonable overhead. The diamond spin qubits operate at 10 Kelvin, warmer than the millikelvin temperatures required by superconducting qubits, and the team plans to scale up by adding more nuclear spins and developing optical interconnects for networking.

In late February, Amazon Web Services (AWS) unveiled Ocelot, its first prototype quantum computing chip focused on error correction. Ocelot uses novel “bosonic cat qubits”—a type of qubit encoded in harmonic oscillator states that are naturally resistant to bit-flip errors. The chip uses a one-dimensional repetition code that AWS claims reduces error correction overhead by up to 90% compared to traditional surface codes.

The numbers are striking:

  • Traditional approach: ~49 physical qubits needed for one logical qubit
  • Ocelot approach: 9 physical qubits needed (5 data qubits, 4 ancilla qubits)

Ocelot’s cat qubits maintain bit-flip stability for 1 second—orders of magnitude longer than the 50-100 microsecond coherence times of traditional transmon qubits. The phase-flip time is 20 microseconds, which the system corrects through its repetition code architecture. This hardware-efficient approach could dramatically accelerate progress toward fault-tolerant quantum systems.

Architecture Innovations

MIT researchers developed a novel quantum interconnect that enables all-to-all communication between superconducting quantum processors. The team demonstrated remote entanglement between two processors using a superconducting waveguide, achieving over 60% photon absorption efficiency. This interconnect paves the way for scalable quantum networks and distributed quantum computing by allowing modules to communicate directly without complex routing architectures.

NTT Corporation and collaborators proposed a new load-store architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing that separates memory and processor, similar to classical computer architecture. This approach achieves:

  • Up to 100% asymptotic memory efficiency
  • ~90% practical memory efficiency
  • Only a ~3% increase in computation time compared to ideal systems

This represents a significant improvement over conventional quantum computers, which achieve only 44-67% memory efficiency. The architecture enables more efficient use of quantum hardware and improves program portability across different quantum systems.

Researchers are also exploring alternatives to traditional qubits. Nature highlighted the emerging field of “qudits”—quantum information units that can exist in three or more simultaneous states (compared to qubits’ two states). Qudits offer increased information density and could reduce the number of quantum elements needed for certain computations.

Room-Temperature and Modular Systems

Xanadu launched Aurora, the world’s first modular, room-temperature photonic quantum computer. The system uses:

  • 35 interconnected photonic chips
  • 8 miles (13 kilometers) of fiber optic cables
  • Room-temperature operation—no cryogenic cooling required

Photonic quantum computing uses particles of light rather than matter-based qubits, enabling room-temperature operation and fiber-optic networking. Xanadu’s modular approach tackles scalability and error correction by allowing the system to be expanded through additional modules. The Nature-published architecture could enable practical quantum data centers and new applications in molecular simulation and cryptography.

Company Innovation Key Metric Significance
Fujitsu/QuTech/TU Delft Diamond spin qubits 0.1% error rate Error correction milestone
Amazon (AWS) Ocelot chip with cat qubits 90% overhead reduction Fewer physical qubits needed
Xanadu Aurora modular system Room-temperature operation No cryogenic cooling
MIT Quantum interconnect All-to-all communication Scalable architecture

Ecosystem Development: OS, Networking, and AI Integration

As hardware advances, the quantum ecosystem is maturing with new operating systems, networking capabilities, and integration with classical AI computing.

Quantum Operating Systems

OQTOPUS (Open Quantum Toolchain for Operators and Users), an open-source quantum computer operating system, launched on GitHub from a consortium led by Osaka University, Fujitsu, SEC, and TIS. The OS covers the full stack from quantum computer setup to operation, lowering the barrier to deploying quantum computers via the cloud. Fujitsu plans to make OQTOPUS available to research partners in the second half of 2025.

Separately, researchers published QNodeOS in Nature—a quantum network operating system that enables platform-independent execution of quantum network applications in high-level software. The system was demonstrated on quantum network nodes based on:

  • Nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond (2 nodes)
  • Trapped-ion systems (1 node with a single 40Ca+ atom)

QNodeOS allows multitasking and efficient hardware use, abstracting underlying physical complexities so users can execute applications without detailed knowledge of the specific quantum systems. This work, described as a “huge practical step forward” in a Nature commentary , provides a critical abstraction layer for the emerging quantum internet.

AI + Quantum

NVIDIA announced the NVIDIA Accelerated Quantum Research Center (NVAQC) in Boston to integrate AI supercomputing with quantum computing. The center will deploy 576 Blackwell GPUs and use Quantum-2 InfiniBand networking to tackle challenges like qubit noise and error correction. Partners include Quantinuum, Quantum Machines, QuEra Computing, Harvard University, and MIT.

Interestingly, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang recently estimated that practical quantum computers are likely 20 years away, noting a gap of 5-6 orders of magnitude in qubit count needed for useful systems. Yet NVIDIA is investing now to develop the hybrid quantum-classical systems that will bridge that gap.

On the theoretical side, Google Quantum AI researchers published work showing quantum algorithms could learn “periodic neuron” neural networks exponentially faster than classical methods. The proposed approach uses a modified quantum Fourier transform within a Quantum Statistical Query learning model to find hidden patterns in data. This work is purely theoretical—it doesn’t demonstrate a practical speedup on current hardware—but identifies a specific problem class where quantum computers might offer provable advantages.

Industry-Academia Partnerships

In Germany, Fraunhofer IAO, Fraunhofer IPA, and the University of Stuttgart established “flaQship”, a cross-institute lab to pool research expertise in applied quantum computing. The lab focuses on quantum machine learning, material simulation, and error correction, aiming to create value for companies and society. The collaboration will organize the ML4QT symposium in July 2025 to advance quantum technology through machine learning.

Money and Momentum: The Investment Surge

March revealed the massive capital flowing into quantum computing, with venture funding setting records and governments making strategic bets.

Mega-Rounds

PsiQuantum is raising at least $750 million at a $6 billion valuation to fund its development of million-qubit, fault-tolerant photonic quantum computers. The company is leveraging traditional chip manufacturing at GlobalFoundries and has secured major public partnerships:

  • $500 million from the State of Illinois, Cook County, and Chicago for a U.S. quantum computer project
  • $617 million (AUD $940 million) from Australian governments for a Brisbane computer

PsiQuantum targets 2029 to deliver its first commercial system, positioning it as a competitor to tech giants pursuing different qubit technologies.

China launched a massive $138 billion government-backed venture fund to invest in emerging technologies including quantum computing, AI, and semiconductors. The fund aims to commercialize research and enhance technological self-reliance, dwarfing Western initiatives:

  • U.S. National Quantum Initiative: $1.2 billion over five years (2018), with $2.7 billion proposed for reauthorization
  • Europe’s Quantum Flagship: ~$1.1 billion over 10 years

IonQ raised $372.6 million through a share sale, bringing its total cash balance to over $700 million. The funding follows strategic moves including acquiring a majority stake in quantum networking provider ID Quantique and forming a partnership with SK Telecom. IonQ also commissioned a quantum networking system at the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory as part of over $94.4 million in contracts.

Growth Funding

Smaller but strategically important rounds included:

  • QuamCore (Israel): $9 million seed funding for architecture enabling 1 million superconducting qubits in a single cryostat by reducing cabling by a factor of 1,000
  • QuantWare (Netherlands): 20 million Series A for VIO technology to scale quantum processors to 1 million+ qubits; also launched pre-orders for “Contralto-A” QPU, nearly twice as large as competing solutions
  • Singapore: $18.3 million SGD for HQCC 1.0, a national initiative to integrate quantum and high-performance computing
  • Australia: $15 million government investment in QuintessenceLabs for quantum cybersecurity
  • Iceberg Quantum: $2 million pre-seed and partnership with PsiQuantum to apply quantum LDPC codes for error correction overhead reduction

The broader trend is clear: 2024 set a new venture funding record for quantum computing startups at $1.9 billion, up 138% from 2023’s $789 million, according to Crunchbase data . Momentum continues into 2025 with massive individual rounds including QuEra Computing’s $230 million and Quantum Machines’ $170 million.

Not everyone is keeping pace. A report in The Times warns the UK risks falling behind due to government spending delays, despite strong research from institutions like Oxford University and startups like Oxford Ionics (which has raised 37 million and employs 80 engineers). Competitors including the U.S. and Germany are moving faster with larger contracts.

What March Really Means

Stepping back from individual news items, three patterns emerge from March’s developments:

First, quantum supremacy claims are diversifying. D-Wave demonstrated advantage on a practical materials simulation problem using annealing. China’s Zuchongzhi-3 showed massive speedup on random circuit sampling. Quantinuum and partners proved certified randomness is classically impossible. These aren’t competing claims on a single benchmark—they’re demonstrations of different quantum approaches excelling at different tasks. The field isn’t a single race anymore; it’s branching into multiple technological paths.

Second, skepticism is healthy. The controversy around Microsoft’s Majorana 1 chip shows the field is maturing and demanding rigorous evidence. After past retractions and exaggerated claims, physicists are rightfully insisting on extraordinary evidence for extraordinary breakthroughs. This skepticism doesn’t slow progress—it strengthens it by ensuring resources flow to reproducible, verifiable advances.

Third, the real story is money. $1.9 billion in 2024 VC funding (up 138%), massive government investments like China’s $138 billion fund, and huge bets on specific approaches like PsiQuantum’s $750 million for photonics and D-Wave’s annealing systems. The debate has shifted from “will quantum work?” to “which approach will scale?”

March didn’t resolve the fundamental questions in quantum computing. Error correction remains challenging, practical applications are still emerging, and timelines for fault-tolerant systems span years to decades. But the month clarified the stakes: companies and countries are placing substantial bets on different technological approaches, hardware is making measurable progress on error correction and scaling, and the ecosystem is developing the software and infrastructure needed to make quantum computers usable.

The race isn’t about a single breakthrough anymore—it’s about which combination of qubit technology, error correction approach, and ecosystem development reaches practical scale first. March brought progress on all three fronts.

This comprehensive review covers 3 articles published between February 1 and February 26, 2025, surveying how artificial intelligence is transforming materials science. Research reviews demonstrate accelerated discovery in MXenes and perovskites, while industry data reveals 74% of chemical companies are now deploying AI in R&D.

Research Spotlight: Computational Methods Accelerate Discovery

Two review articles published this month document how computational methods are accelerating materials discovery, demonstrating a consistent pattern: artificial intelligence and first-principles calculations work together to guide experimental work.

MXenes: Computational Prediction Guides Experiment

MXenes , a family of 2D transition metal carbides and nitrides discovered in 2011, have seen interest grow at 34% annually according to a review in npj Computational Materials . This rapid growth creates a challenge: researchers must navigate an exponentially expanding design space to identify promising compositions for specific applications.

The review highlights how density functional theory (DFT) and machine learning are being used together to predict MXene properties before synthesis. DFT calculations allow researchers to explore electronic structure, surface chemistry, and mechanical properties across the MXene family. Various functionals appear in the literature, including PBE, TPSS, M06, B3LYP, PBE0, HSE06, and others from Perdew’s “Jacob’s ladder” of density functional approximations.

Machine learning complements these first-principles calculations by learning patterns from computed datasets, enabling faster prediction of properties for new MXene compositions. This computational guidance helps narrow the vast design space, directing experimental synthesis toward the most promising candidates. The review notes that despite progress, challenges remain in transitioning MXenes from laboratory demonstrations to practical applications.

Perovskites: Automation Drives Efficiency Gains

Perovskite photovoltaics present a similar story of computational acceleration. Since their emergence in 2009, perovskite solar cells have seen power conversion efficiency rise from 3.8% to over 26%, according to a review in InfoMat . This rapid improvement has been driven partly by machine learning and automation.

The review, authored by researchers from Forschungszentrum Jülich, Helmholtz-Institute Erlangen-Nürnberg (HI ERN), and the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC), describes how Autonomous Material and Device Acceleration Platforms (AMADAP) enable high-throughput experimentation. These automated systems can prepare samples, test devices, and feed results back into machine learning models that suggest the next experiment.

Materials with the \(ABX_3\) perovskite structure present optimization challenges due to the vast parameter space of compositions, processing conditions, and device architectures. ML-driven automation addresses this by exploring more combinations faster than manual methods allow. The review notes various deposition techniques being automated, including spin-coating, doctor-blading, and spray-coating.

Both MXenes and perovskites demonstrate the same underlying pattern: computational methods don’t replace experimentation, but they make it more efficient by predicting what to try next.

Industry Adoption: AI Moves from Lab to Production

The computational methods documented in academic research are now being deployed at scale across the chemicals industry. According to an analysis by Elsevier , 74% of chemical companies have begun implementing AI in their R&D processes. This finding comes from an IBM survey of 400 chemicals executives, 80% of whom said AI will be important to their business in the next three years.

The article highlights a concrete example from Dow Polyurethane, where AI has transformed foam formulation development. Previously, developing new flexible foam formulations took experts 4 to 6 months of iterative testing. With AI, this process now takes seconds. Rather than replacing the experts, the AI augments their capabilities, allowing them to explore more options and reach optimal formulations faster.

McKinsey & Company estimates that generative AI could create $140 billion in value across the energy and materials sector by accelerating the identification of new molecules and formulations. This potential is driving rapid adoption, but the article emphasizes that success depends on a critical foundation: data.

**FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable)] are essential for effective AI deployment. Elsevier works with companies like Johnson Matthey to build “data scaffolding” through enrichment, knowledge graphs, and semantic search. SciBite, an Elsevier company, provides semantic technology to structure chemical and biological data for AI applications.

The article also mentions broader AI initiatives in the industry, including Microsoft and Surveily using AI for predictive maintenance and safety monitoring in chemical plants. These applications extend beyond R&D into operations, showing AI’s potential to improve safety and sustainability alongside accelerating innovation.

The Pattern: Integration, Not Replacement

The three articles from February reveal a consistent theme: AI is integrating into materials science and chemical engineering as an augmentation tool, not a replacement for expertise. In academic research, DFT calculations guide MXene synthesis exploration, and ML-driven automation accelerates perovskite efficiency improvements. In industry, AI formulations tools reduce development time from months to seconds, but experts remain in the loop.

The common thread across all these developments is the integration of computational methods with domain knowledge. DFT + ML for MXenes, automation + ML for perovskites, and AI + expert formulation guidance at Dow all follow the same pattern: the technology augments, accelerates, and extends what human researchers can achieve.

Success depends on foundations that aren’t glamorous but are essential: high-quality computational data for training ML models, FAIR-compliant data infrastructure in industry, and experimental validation of computational predictions. As the survey data shows, the chemicals industry has moved beyond asking whether AI is useful to asking how to deploy it effectively. The research literature suggests materials science is following the same trajectory.

item.description: This comprehensive review covers 95 selected articles from 204 published in February 2025, surveying a month of unprecedented developments in quantum computing. In a single month, the quantum computing landscape shifted dramatically. Microsoft unveiled a topological qubit chip after 17 years of research. Amazon revealed its first quantum processor with game-changing error correction. Oxford scientists demonstrated distributed quantum computing via teleportation.
